bio.en: Ronny Kohavi is widely regarded as the world's leading expert on A/B testing and experimentation, formerly VP and Technical Fellow of Relevance at Airbnb, Corporate VP at Microsoft, and Director of Data Mining at Amazon, and author of Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments.
bio.zh: Ronny Kohavi 被公认为全球 A/B 测试与实验领域的顶尖专家，曾任 Airbnb 相关性副总裁兼技术研究员、微软公司副总裁、亚马逊数据挖掘总监，也是《可信在线受控实验》一书的作者。

summary.en: Ronny makes the case for 'test everything,' sharing the famous Bing story where moving one search line increased revenue by ~12% ($100M) and the Airbnb new-tab experiment. He explains why most predictions about experiments are humblingly wrong, how to build a culture of trustworthy experimentation, and why trust is the most important element of a successful program. The episode is a tactical masterclass on running experiments that actually move metrics.
summary.zh: Ronny 力主“凡事皆测试”，分享了著名的 Bing 案例——仅仅移动一行搜索结果就带来约 12%（1 亿美元）的营收增长——以及 Airbnb 新标签页实验。他解释了为什么我们对实验结果的预测常常错得离谱，如何建立可信实验的文化，以及为什么“信任”是成功实验体系中最关键的要素。本期是关于运行真正能撬动指标的实验的实战大师课。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I'm very clear that I'm a big fan of test everything, which is any code change that you make, any feature that you introduce has to be in some experiment. Because again, I've observed this sort of surprising result that even small bug fixes, even small changes can sometimes have surprising, unexpected impact.
turns.zh: 我很明确我是一个“测试一切”的大力倡导者——也就是说，你做的任何代码改动、你引入的任何功能，都必须放在某种实验中。因为再说一次，我观察到这种令人惊讶的结果：即使是小的 bug 修复、即使是小的改动，有时也会带来出人意料、意想不到的影响。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And so I don't think it's possible to experiment too much. You have to allocate sometimes to these high risk, high reward ideas. We're going to try something that's most likely to fail. But if it does win, it's going to be a home run.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得实验是没办法做得太过的。你有时得把资源分配到那些高风险、高回报的想法上。我们要去试那些最可能失败的东西。但如果它赢了，那会是个全垒打（本垒打）。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And you have to be ready to understand and agree that most will fail. And it's amazing how many times I've seen people come up with new designs or a radical new idea. And they believe in it, and that's okay. I'm just cautioning them all the time to say, "If you go for something big, try it out, but be ready to fail 80% of the time."
turns.zh: 而你必须准备好去理解并认同：大多数会失败。我见过太多次，人们想出新设计或激进的新想法。他们相信它，那没关系。我只是不断提醒他们：“如果你去搏大的，去试，但要准备好 80% 的时候会失败。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ronny, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Ronny，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Thank you for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you're known by many as maybe the leading expert on A/B testing and experimentation, which I think is something every product company eventually ends up trying to do, often badly. And so I'm excited to dig quite deep into the world of experimentation and A/B testing to help people run better experiments. So thank you again for being here.
turns.zh: 所以你被很多人视为也许是 A/B 测试和实验的顶尖专家，而我觉得这是每个产品公司最终都会尝试去做的事，而且常常做得很糟。所以我很兴奋能深入挖掘实验和 A/B 测试的世界，帮助人们跑更好的实验。所以再次感谢你来到这里。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: That's a great goal. Thank you.
turns.zh: 那是个很棒的目标。谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me start with kind of a fun question. What is maybe the most unexpected A/B tests you've run or maybe the most surprising result from an A/B test that you've run?
turns.zh: 让我从一个挺有趣的问题开始。也许你跑过的最意外的 A/B 测试是什么，或者你跑过的最令人惊讶的结果是什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So I think the opening example that I use in my book and in my class is the most surprising public example we can talk about. And this was kind of an interesting experiment. Somebody proposed to change the way that ads were displayed on Bing, the search engine. And he basically said, "Let's take the second line and move it, promote it to the first line so that the title line becomes larger."
turns.zh: 我觉得我在书和课上用的开篇例子，是我们可以聊的最令人惊讶的公开例子。这是个挺有意思的实验。有人提议改变 Bing 这个搜索引擎上广告的展示方式。他基本上说“我们把第二行拿过来，提升到第一行，这样标题行变得更大。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And when you think about that, and if you're going to look in my book, or in the class, there's an actual diagram of what happened, the screenshots. But if you think about it, just realistically it looks like a meh idea. Why would this be such a reasonable, interesting thing to do? And indeed, when we went back to the backlog, it was on the backlog for months, and languished there, and many things were rated higher.
turns.zh: 当你想到这个，如果你去看我的书或课，里面有个实际发生情况的图示、截图。但如果你现实地想，它看起来像个“也就那样”的想法。为什么这会是个这么合理、有趣的事去做？而事实上，当我们回到 backlog，它在 backlog 里待了好几个月，被冷落着，很多东西被评得更高。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: But the point about this is it's trivial to implement. So if you think about return on investment, we could get the data by having some engineers spend a couple of hours implementing it.
turns.zh: 但关于这个的关键点是，它实现起来微不足道。所以如果你考虑投资回报率，我们可以让一些工程师花几个小时实现它，就能拿到数据。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And that's exactly what happened. Somebody at Bing who kept seeing this in the backlog and said, "My God, we're spending too much time discussing it. I could just implement it." He did. He spent a couple of days implementing it, as is the common thing at Bing, he launched the experiment.
turns.zh: 而那正是发生的事。Bing 里有人一直看到这个在 backlog 里，说“我的天，我们花太多时间讨论它了。我直接实现它就行了。”他做了。他花几天实现了它，按照 Bing 常见的做法，他启动了实验。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And a funny thing happened. We had an alarm. Big escalation, something is wrong with the revenue metric. Now this alarm fired several times in the past when there were real mistakes, where somebody would log revenue twice, or there's some data problem. But in this case, there was no bug. That simple idea increased revenue by about 12%.
turns.zh: 然后一个有趣的事发生了。我们触发了一个警报。重大升级：收入指标出了点问题。现在这个警报过去在真有错误时触发过几次——有人把收入记了两次，或有些数据问题。但这次，没有 bug。那个简单的想法让收入增加了约 12%。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And this is something that just doesn't happen. We can talk later about Wyman's law, but that was the first reaction, which is, "This is too good to be true. Let's find a bug." And we did. And we looked for several times, and we replicated the experiment several times, and there was nothing wrong with it. This thing was worth $100 million at the time when Bing was a lot smaller.
turns.zh: 而这是那种就是不会发生的事。我们后面可以聊 Wyman 定律，但那是最初的反应——“这好得不像真的。找 bug 去。”而我们确实找了。我们找了好几次，并重复了实验好几次，而它没有任何问题。这个东西在当时 Bing 还小得多的时候，价值 1 亿美元。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And the key thing is it didn't hurt the user metrics. So it's very easy to increase revenue by doing theatrics. Displaying more ads is a trivial way to raise revenue, but it hurts the user experience. And we've done the experiments to show that. In this case, this was just a home run that improved revenue, didn't significantly hurt the guardrail metrics. And so we were in awe of what a trivial change. That was the biggest revenue impact to Bing in all its history.
turns.zh: 而关键点是它没有伤害用户指标。所以通过花哨手段来增加收入是非常容易的。展示更多广告是个提升收入的琐碎方式，但它伤害用户体验。而我们已经做过实验来证明那个。这个 case 里，这是个全垒打，提升了收入，又没显著伤害护栏指标。于是我们对一个微不足道的改动竟有如此效果感到敬畏。那是 Bing 历史上最大的收入影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that was basically shifting in two lines, right? Switching two lines in the search results.
turns.zh: 而那基本就是挪动两行，对吧？在搜索结果里交换两行。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And this was just moving the second line to the first line. Now you then go and run a lot of experiments to understand what happened here. Is it the fact that the title line has a bigger font, sometimes different color? So we ran a whole bunch of experiments.
turns.zh: 而这只是把第二行移到了第一行。然后你去跑大量实验来理解这里发生了什么。是因为标题行有更大的字体、有时不同颜色吗？所以我们跑了一大堆实验。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And this is what usually happens. We have a breakthrough. You start to understand more about, what can we do? And there suddenly a shift towards, "Okay, what are other things we could do that would allow us to improve revenue?" We came up with a lot of follow on ideas that helped a lot.
turns.zh: 而这是通常会发生的事。我们有个突破。你开始更多地理解，我们能做什么？然后突然转向“好，我们还能做哪些别的事，让我们能提升收入？”我们想出了一大堆后续想法，帮了大忙。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: But to me, this was an example of a tiny change that was the best revenue generating idea in Bing's history, and we didn't rate it properly. Nobody gave this the priority that in hindsight, it deserves. And that's something that happens often. I mean, we are often humbled by how bad we are at predicting the outcome of experiments.
turns.zh: 但对我来说，这是个小改动成为 Bing 历史上最佳创收想法的例子，而我们没有正确地给它评级。没人给这个它在事后应得的优先级。而那是经常发生的事。我的意思是，我们常常被自己在预测实验结果上有多差给“ humility（谦卑）”到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of a classic experiment at Airbnb while I was there, and we'll talk about Airbnb in a bit. The search team just ran a small experiment of what if we were to open a new tab every time someone clicked on a search result, instead of just going straight to that listing. And that was one of the biggest wins in search-
turns.zh: 这让我想起我在 Airbnb 时一个经典的实验，我们稍后会聊 Airbnb。搜索团队就跑了一个小实验：如果我们每次有人点击搜索结果时都打开一个新标签页，而不是直接跳到那个房源，会怎样。那是搜索领域最大的胜利之一——

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And by the way, I don't know if you know the history of this, but I tell about this in class. We did this experiment way back around 2008 I think. And so this predates Airbnb. I remember it was heavily debated. Why would you open something in a new tab? The users didn't ask for it. It was a lot of pushback from the designers. And we ran that experiment. And again, it was one of these highly surprising results that made it that we learned so much from it.
turns.zh: 顺便，我不知道你是否知道这个的历史，但我在课上会讲这个。我们早在大概 2008 年就做了这个实验。所以它早于 Airbnb。我记得当时争议很大。为什么要开新标签？用户又没要求。设计师那边有很多阻力。而我们跑了那个实验。而再次，它是那些高度令人惊讶的结果之一，让我们从中学习良多。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So we first did this. It was done in the UK for opening Hotmail, and then we moved it to MSN, so it would open search in new tab, and all the set of experiments were highly, highly beneficial. We published this. And I have to tell you, when I came to Airbnb, I talked to our joint friend Ricardo about this. And it was sort of done, it was very beneficial, and then it was semi forgotten, which is one of the things you learned about institutional memories. When you have winners, make sure to address them and remember them. So it was at Airbnb done for a long time before I joined that listings opened in a new tab, but other things that were designed in the future were not done. And I reintroduced this to the team, and we saw big improvements.
turns.zh: 所以我们先做了这个。它是在英国为打开 Hotmail 做的，然后我们移到 MSN，这样它会开新标签搜索，而那一整套实验都高度、高度有益。我们发表了这个。而我得告诉你，当我到 Airbnb 时，我和我们共同的朋友 Ricardo 聊了这个。它当时算是做了，非常有益，然后它被半遗忘——这是你从机构记忆（institutional memory）学到的事之一。当你有赢家时，要确保去处理它们、记住它们。所以 Airbnb 在我加入前很长时间就把房源开在新标签了，但未来设计的别的东西没做。而我向团队重新引入了这个，我们看到了很大的改进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shout out to Ricardo, our mutual friend who helped make this conversation happen. There's this holy grail of experiments that I think people are always looking for of one hour of work and it creates this massive result. I imagine this is very rare, and don't expect this to happen. I guess in your experience, how often do you find one of these gold nuggets just lying around?
turns.zh: 为我们的共同朋友 Ricardo 喊一声，他帮忙促成了这次对话。有一个人们一直在找的实验圣杯：一小时的工作，却创造出巨大的结果。我想象这非常罕见，别指望这个会发生。我想在你经验里，你多久能找到一个就这样躺在那里的金块？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah. So again, this is a topic that's near and dear to my heart. Everybody wants these amazing results, and I show them in chapter one in my book, multiple of these small efforts, huge gain.
turns.zh: 是的。所以再次，这是个贴近我心的主题。每个人都想要这些惊人的结果，而我在书的第一章展示了好几个：小小的努力，巨大的收获。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: But as you said, they're very rare. I think most of the time, the winnings are made this inch by inch. And there's a graph that I show in my book, a real graph of how Bing ads has managed to improve the revenue per a thousand searches over time, and every month you can see a small improvement and a small improvement. Sometimes the degradation because of legal reasons or other things. There were some concern that we were not marking the ads properly. So you have to suddenly do something that you know is going to hurt revenue. But yes, I think most results are inch by inch. You improve small amounts, lots of them. I think that the best example that I can say is a couple of them that I can speak about.
turns.zh: 但正如你说的，它们非常罕见。我觉得大多数时候，胜利是一寸一寸取得的。我的书里有一张图，一张真实的图，展示 Bing 广告如何随着时间改善每千次搜索的收入，你能看到每个月都有小的改善、小的改善。有时因为法律原因或其他而退化。有些顾虑是我们没把广告标好。所以你有时得突然做你知道会伤害收入的事。但是的，我觉得大多数结果是一寸一寸的。你改善很小的量，很多次。我觉得我能说的最好的例子是几个我能谈的。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: One is at Bing, the relevance team, hundreds of people all working to improve bing relevance. They have a metric, we'll talk about OEC, the overall evaluation criterion. But they have a metric that their goal is to improve it by 2% every year. It's a small amount, and that 2% you can see here's a 0.1, and here's a 0.15, here's a 0.2, and then they add up to around 2% every year, which is amazing.
turns.zh: 一个是在 Bing，相关性团队，数百人都在努力改善 Bing 的相关性。他们有一个指标，我们稍后会聊 OEC，即总体评估标准（overall evaluation criterion）。但他们有一个指标，目标是每年改善 2%。这是个小数，而那 2% 你能看到这里是 0.1、这里是 0.15、这里是 0.2，然后它们加起来每年大概 2%，这很惊人。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Another example that I am allowed to speak about from Airbnb is the fact that we ran some 250 experiments in my tenure there in search relevance. And again, small improvements added up. So this became overall a 6% improvement to revenue. So when you think about 6%, it's a big number, but it came out not of one idea, but many, many smaller ideas that each gave you a small gain.
turns.zh: 另一个我可以说、来自 Airbnb 的例子是：我在那里的任期内，我们在搜索相关性上跑了大约 250 个实验。再次，小的改善累积起来。所以总体而言成了对收入 6% 的改善。所以当你想到 6%，这是个大数据，但它不是来自一个想法，而是来自许多、许多更小的想法，每一个都给你小的收获。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And in fact, again, there's another number I'm allowed to say. Of these experiments, 92% failed to improve the metric that we were trying to move. So only 8% of our ideas actually were successful at moving the key metrics.
turns.zh: 而事实上，还有另一个我可以说的数据。在这些实验里，92% 未能改善我们试图推动的那个指标。所以只有 8% 的想法真正成功地推动了关键指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many threads I want to follow here, but let me follow this one right here. You just mentioned of 92% of experiments failed. Is that typical in your experience seeing experiments running a lot of companies? What should people expect when they're running experiments? What percentage should they expect to fail?
turns.zh: 这里有好多线索我想顺着追，但让我就顺着这个。你刚提到 92% 的实验失败了。这在你看到很多公司跑实验的经验里典型吗？人们跑实验时应该预期什么？他们应该预期多少百分比失败？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Well, first of all, I published three different numbers for my career. So overall at Microsoft, about 66%, two thirds of ideas fail. And don't think the 66 is accurate. It's about two thirds. At Bing, which is a much more optimized domain after we've been optimizing it for a while, the failure rate was around 85%. So it's harder to improve something that you've been optimizing for a while. And then at Airbnb, this 92% number is the highest failure rate that I've observed.
turns.zh: 好，首先，我为我职业生涯发表了三个不同的数字。所以整体在微软，大约 66%，三分之二的想法失败。别以为那 66 是精确数。大概是三分之二。在 Bing，那是个被优化得多的领域——在我们优化了一阵之后——失败率大约在 85%。所以改善一个你已优化了一阵的东西更难。然后在 Airbnb，这个 92% 的数字是我观察到的最高失败率。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Now I've quoted other sources. It's not that I worked at groups that were particularly bad, Booking, Google Ads, other companies published numbers that are around 80 to 90% failure rate of ideas. This is where it's important of experiments. It's important to realize that when you have a platform, it's easy to get this number. You look at how many experiments were run and how many of them launched. Not every experiment maps to an idea.
turns.zh: 现在我也引用过其他来源。不是我所在的组特别差——Booking、Google Ads、其他公司发表的数字大约也是想法 80% 到 90% 的失败率。这正是实验重要的地方。重要的是意识到，当你有一个平台时，拿到这个数字很容易。你看跑了多少实验、其中多少上线了。不是每个实验都对应一个想法。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So it's possible that when you have an idea, your first implementation, you start an experiment. Boom, it's egregiously bad, because you have a bug. In fact, 10% of experiments tend to be aborted on the first date. Those are usually not that the idea is bad, but that there is an implementation issue or something we haven't thought about, that forces an abort.
turns.zh: 所以可能你有一个想法，你的第一次实现，你启动一个实验。砰，它糟得离谱，因为你有 bug。事实上，10% 的实验往往在第一次就中止了。那些通常不是想法糟，而是有实现问题或我们没考虑到的东西，迫使中止。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: You may iterate and pivot again. And ultimately, if you do two, or three, or four pivots or bug fixes, you may get to a successful launch. But those numbers of 80 to 92% failure rate are of experiments.
turns.zh: 你可能迭代并再次转向。最终，如果你做了两、三或四次转向或 bug 修复，你可能达到一个成功的上线。但那些 80% 到 92% 的失败率，是实验的失败率。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Very humbling. I know that every group that starts to run experiments, they always start off by thinking that somehow, they're different. And their success rate's going to be much, much higher, and they're all humbled.
turns.zh: 非常让人谦卑。我知道每个开始跑实验的组，一开始都以为自己不知怎的有点不同。他们的成功率会高得多高得多，而他们都变得谦卑了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned that you had this pattern of clicking a link and opening a new tab as a thing that just worked at a lot of different places.
turns.zh: 你提到你有这个点击链接开新标签的模式，作为一个在很多不同地方都奏效的东西。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there other versions of this? Do you do you collect a list of, "Here's things that often work when we want to move" there's some you could share. I don't know if you have a list in your head.
turns.zh: 还有别的这种版本吗？你会不会收集一个清单，“这里是我们想推动时经常奏效的东西”，有什么你能分享的。我不知道你脑子里有没有个清单。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I can give you two resources. One of them is a paper that we wrote called Rules of Thumb, and what we tried to do at that time at Microsoft was to just look at thousands of experiments that run and extract some patterns. And so that's one paper that we can then put in the notes.
turns.zh: 我可以给你两个资源。一个是我们在微软时写的一篇叫《经验法则》（Rules of Thumb）的论文，我们当时尝试的就是看数千个跑过的实验，提取一些模式。所以那是我们可以放进笔记里的一篇论文。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: But there's another more accurate, I would say, resource that's useful that I recommend to people. And it's a site called goodui.org, and goodui.org is exactly the site that tries to do what you're saying at scale.
turns.zh: 但还有另一个更准确、我会说更有用的资源，我推荐给人们。它是个叫 goodui.org 的网站，而 goodui.org 正是那种试图在规模上做你说的那种事的网站。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So guy's name is Jacob [inaudible 00:16:28]. He asks people to send them results of experiments, and he puts them into patterns. There's probably 140 patterns I think at this point. And then for each pattern he says, "Well, who has that helped? How many times and by how much?" So you have an idea of this worked, three out of five times. And it was a huge win. In fact, you can find that open a new window in there.
turns.zh: 一个叫 Jacob 的人[听不清 00:16:28]。他让人们把实验结果发给他，然后他把它们整合成模式。到这点上大概有 140 个模式了。然后对每个模式他说“好，谁从中受益了？多少次、多大程度？”所以你有个概念：这个奏效了，五分之三的时候。而那是个巨大的胜利。事实上，你能在那里找到“开新窗口”那条。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you feed that into ChatGPT, and you have basically a product manager creating a roadmap tool.
turns.zh: 我觉得你把这喂给 ChatGPT，你基本就有了一个产品经理在创建路线图工具。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: In general, by the way, a lot of that is institutional memory, which is can you document things well enough so that the organization remembers the successes and failures, and learns from them?
turns.zh: 总的来说，顺便说，那很多是机构记忆，也就是你能不能把事情记录得足够好，让组织记住成功和失败，并从中学习？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I think one of the mistakes that some company makes is they launch a lot of experiments and never go back and summarize the learnings. So I've actually put a lot of effort in this idea of institutional learning, of doing the quarterly meeting of the most surprising experiments.
turns.zh: 我觉得有些公司犯的一个错误是，他们跑了一大堆实验，却从不回过头去总结学到的东西。所以我在“机构学习”这个想法上其实花了很多精力——做最令人惊讶的实验的季度会议。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: By the way, surprising is another question that people often are not clear about. What is a surprising experiment? To me, a surprising experiment is one where the estimated result beforehand and the actual result differ by a lot. So that absolute value of the difference is large.
turns.zh: 顺便，令人惊讶是另一个人们常常不清楚的问题。什么是一个令人惊讶的实验？对我来说，一个令人惊讶的实验是：事先估计的结果和真实结果相差很大。所以那个差值的绝对值很大。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Now you can expect something to be great and it's flat. Well, you learn something. But if you expect something to be small and it turns out to be great, like that ad title promotion, then you've learned a lot. Or conversely, if you expect that something will be small and it's very negative, you can learn a lot by understanding why this was so negative. And that's interesting.
turns.zh: 现在你可能预期某物会很棒而它是平的。嗯，你学到了点东西。但如果你预期某物很小、结果它却很棒，像那个广告标题提升，那你学到了很多。或者反过来，如果你预期某物会很小而它非常负面，你可以通过理解为什么这么负面学到很多。而那很有趣。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So we focused not just on the winners, but also surprising losers, things that people thought would be a no-brainer to run. And then for some reason, it was very negative. And sometimes, it's that negative that gives you insight. Actually, I'm just coming up with one example that of that, that I should mention.
turns.zh: 所以我们不只聚焦赢家，也聚焦令人惊讶的输家——那些人们以为跑起来是板上钉钉的事。然后出于某种原因，它非常负面。而有时，正是那个负面给了你洞见。其实，我正想到一个我该提的、那类的例子。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: We were running this experiment at Microsoft to improve the windows indexer, and the team was able to show on offline tests that it does much better at indexing, and they showed some relevance is higher, and all these good things. And then they ran it as an experiment. You know what happened? Surprising result. Indexing the relevance was actually high, but it killed a battery life.
turns.zh: 我们在微软跑过一个实验来改善 Windows 索引器，团队能在离线测试里展示它在索引上做得好得多，他们展示了一些相关性更高、以及所有这些好东西。然后他们把它作为实验跑了。你知道发生了什么吗？令人惊讶的结果。索引的相关性确实高，但它把电池续航给搞死了。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So here's something that comes from left field that you didn't expect. It was consuming a lot more CPU on laptops. It was killing the laptops. And therefore, okay, we learned something. Let's document it. Let's remember this, so that we now take this other factor into account as we design the next iteration.
turns.zh: 所以这是来自左外野、你没预期的东西。它在笔记本上消耗了多得多的 CPU。它在搞死笔记本。所以，好，我们学到了点东西。让我们记录下来。让我们记住这个，这样我们现在设计下一次迭代时把这个别的因素考虑进去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What advice do you have for people to actually remember these surprises? You said that a lot of it is institutional. What do you recommend people do so that they can actually remember this when people leave, say three years later?
turns.zh: 你有什么建议让人们真的记住这些惊讶？你说那很多是机构性的。你推荐人们做什么，才能真的在人们离开、比如三年后，还记住这个？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Document it. We had a large deck internally of these successes and failures, and we encourage people to look at them. The other thing that's very beneficial is just to have your whole history of experiments and do some ability to search by keywords.
turns.zh: 记录下来。我们内部有一大份这些成功和失败的幻灯片，我们鼓励人们去看。另一件非常有益的事，就是拥有你整个实验的历史，并能按关键词搜索。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So I have an idea. Type a few keywords and see if from the thousands of experiments that ran... And by the way, these are very reasonable numbers. At Microsoft, just to let you know, when I left in 2019, we were on a rate of about 20 to 25,000 experiments every year. So every working, day we were starting something like 100 new treatments. Big numbers. So when you're running in a group like Bing, which is running thousands and thousands of experiments, you want to be able to ask, "Has anybody did an experiment on this or this or this?" And so that searching capability is in the platform.
turns.zh: 所以我有个想法。输几个关键词，看看这跑过的数千个实验里……顺便，这些都是很合理的数字。在微软，就让你知道，我 2019 年离开时，我们的速率大概是每年 2 万到 2.5 万个实验。所以每个工作日我们大概在启动 100 个新的处理（treatment）。大数字。所以当你在一个像 Bing 那样跑成千上万个实验的组里，你会希望能问“有没有人对这个或这个或这个做过实验？”而那个搜索能力是内建在平台里的。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: But more than that, I think just doing the quarterly meeting of the most successful... Most interesting, sorry, not just successful, most interesting experiments is very key. And that also helps the flywheel of experimentation.
turns.zh: 但比那更重要的是，我觉得做最成功的……最有趣的——抱歉，不只是成功，是最有趣的实验的季度会议，非常关键。而那也有助实验的飞轮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a good segue to something I wanted to touch on, which is there's often, I guess a weariness of running too many experiments and being too data-driven, and the sense that experimentation just leads you to these micro optimizations, and you don't really innovate and do big things. What's your perspective on that? And then, can you be too experiment driven in your experience?
turns.zh: 这是个好过渡，引向我想要触碰到的一件事：经常有种——我猜是对跑太多实验、太数据驱动的厌倦，以及一种感觉——实验只是把你引向这些微优化，而你并不真的创新、做大事。你对此的视角是什么？然后，在你的经验里，你能不能太以实验为驱动？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I'm very clear that I'm a big fan of test everything, which is any code change that you make, any feature that you introduce has to be in some experiment. Because again, I've observed this surprising result that even small bug fixes, even small changes can sometimes have surprising unexpected impact.
turns.zh: 我很明确我是一个“测试一切”的大力倡导者——也就是说，你做的任何代码改动、你引入的任何功能，都必须放在某种实验中。因为再说一次，我观察到这种令人惊讶的结果：即使是小的 bug 修复、即使是小的改动，有时也会带来出人意料、意想不到的影响。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And so I don't think it's possible to experiment too much. I think it is possible to focus on incremental changes because some people say, "Well, if we only tested 17 things around this," you have to think about, it's like in stock. You need a portfolio. You need some experiments that are incremental that move you in the direction that you know you're going to be successful over time if you just try enough. But some experiments, you have to allocate sometimes to these high risk, high reward ideas. We're going to try something that's most likely to fail, but if it does win, it's going to be a home run.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得实验是没办法做得太过的。我觉得有可能只聚焦在增量改动上，因为有些人说“呃，如果我们只围绕这个测试 17 件事”，你得想，这就像在股票里。你需要一个投资组合。你需要一些增量的实验，把你推向你知道只要试得够多、长期就会成功的方向。但有些实验，你得有时把资源分配到那些高风险、高回报的想法上。我们要去试那些最可能失败的东西。但如果它赢了，那会是个全垒打。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And so you have to allocate some efforts to that, and you have to be ready to understand and agree that most will fail. And I've amazing how many times I've seen people come up with new designs, or a radical new idea, and they believe in it, and that's okay. I'm just cautioning them all the time to say, "Hey, if you go for something big, try it out, but be ready to fail 80% of the time."
turns.zh: 所以你得分配一些精力给那个，而你必须准备好去理解并认同：大多数会失败。我见过太多次，人们想出新设计、或激进的新想法，他们相信它，那没关系。我只是不断提醒他们：“嘿，如果你去搏大的，去试，但要准备好 80% 的时候会失败。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And one true example, that again, I'm able to talk about because we put it in my book, is we were at Bing trying to change the landscape of search. And one of the ideas, the big ideas was we are going to integrate with social. So we hooked into the Twitter fire hose feed and we hooked into Facebook, and we spent 100 person years on this idea.
turns.zh: 而一个真实的例子，再次，我能谈是因为我们把它放进了我的书——我们在 Bing 试图改变搜索的格局。其中一个大想法是我们要和社交整合。所以我们接入了 Twitter 的 fire hose feed，接入了 Facebook，而在这个想法上我们花了 100 人年。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And it failed. You don't see it anymore. It existed for about a year and a half, and all the experiments were just negative to flat. And it was an attempt. It was fair to try it. I think it took us a little long to fail, to decide that this is a failure. But at least we had the data. We had hundreds of experiments that we tried. None of them were a breakthrough. And I remember mailing Qi Lu with some statistics showing that it's time to abort, it's time to fail on this. And he decided to continue more. And it's a million dollar question. Do you continue, and then maybe the breakthrough will come next month, or do you abort? And a few months later, we aborted.
turns.zh: 而它失败了。你不再看到它了。它存在了大约一年半，而所有实验都只是负面到持平。那是一次尝试。试它是公平的。我觉得我们花了稍长的时间才失败、才决定这是个失败。但至少我们有数据。我们试了数百个实验。没有一个突破。而我记得给 Qi Lu 发了邮件，附了些统计，表明是时候中止了、是时候在这个上失败了。而他决定继续更多。而那是个百万美元的问题。你继续，也许突破下个月就来，还是你中止？几个月后，我们中止了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me of at Netflix, they tried a social component that also failed. At Airbnb, early on there was a big social attempt to make, "Here's your friends that have stayed at these Airbnbs," completely had no impact. So maybe that's one of these learnings that we should document.
turns.zh: 那让我想起在 Netflix，他们也试过一个社交组件，也同样失败了。在 Airbnb，早期有个大的社交尝试，想做“这是你那些住过这些 Airbnb 的朋友”，完全没影响。所以也许那是我们该记录下来的一类经验。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah, this is hard. This is hard. But again, that's the value of experiments, which are this oracle that gives you the data. You may be excited about things. You may believe it's a good idea. But ultimately, the oracle is the controlled experiment. It tells you whether users are actually benefiting from it, whether you and the users, the company and the users.
turns.zh: 是的，这很难。这很难。但再次，那正是实验的价值——它这个神谕给你数据。你可能对某些东西很兴奋。你可能相信它是个好想法。但最终，神谕就是受控实验。它告诉你用户是否真的从中受益，你和用户、公司和用户之间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's obviously a bit of overhead and downside to running an experiment, setting all up, and analyzing the results. Is there anything that you ever don't think is worth A/B testing?
turns.zh: 运行一个实验、把它全部搭起来、并分析结果，显然有些开销和弊端。有没有什么是你觉得根本不值得做 A/B 测试的？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: First of all, there are some necessary ingredients to A/B testing. And I'll just say outright, not every domain is amenable to A/B testing. You can't A/B test mergers and acquisitions. It's something that happens once, you either acquire or you don't acquire.
turns.zh: 首先，A/B 测试有一些必要的成分。我直接说，不是每个领域都适合 A/B 测试。你没法对并购做 A/B 测试。那是只发生一次的事，你要么收购要么不收购。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So you do have to have some necessary ingredient. You need to have enough units, mostly users, in order for the statistics to work out. So if you're too small, it may be too early to A/B test. But what I find is that in software, it is so easy to run A/B testing and it is so easy to build a platform.
turns.zh: 所以你确实得有一些必要的成分。你得有足够的单元——主要是用户——好让统计能成立。所以如果你太小，做 A/B 测试可能太早。但我发现的是，在软件里，跑 A/B 测试如此容易，而搭建一个平台也是如此容易。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I don't say it's easy to build a platform. But once you build a platform, the incremental cost of running an experiment should approach zero. And we got to that at Microsoft, where after a while, the cost of running experiments was so low that nobody was questioning the idea that everything should be experimented with.
turns.zh: 我不是说搭建平台容易。但一旦你搭好了平台，跑一个实验的边际成本应该趋近于零。而我们在微软做到了，过了一阵子，跑实验的成本低到没人质疑“一切都应该被实验”这个想法。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Now, I don't think we were there at Airbnb for example. The platform at Airbnb was much less mature, and required a lot more analysts in order to interpret the results and to find issues with it. So I do think there's this trade off. You're willing to invest in the platform. It is possible to get the marginal cost to be close to zero. But when you're not there, it's still expensive, and there may be reasons why not to run A/B tests.
turns.zh: 现在，我觉得在 Airbnb 我们没到那个程度。Airbnb 的平台成熟度低得多，需要多得多的分析师去解读结果、并找出其中的问题。所以我确实觉得这里有个权衡。你愿意投资在平台上。是有可能让边际成本接近零的。但当你没到那一步，它依然昂贵，而可能有理由不跑 A/B 测试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about how you may be too small to run A/B tests, and this is a constant question for startups is, when should we start running A/B tests? Do you have kind of a heuristic or a rule of thumb of, here's a time you should really start thinking about running an A/B test?
turns.zh: 你谈到你可能太小而不适合跑 A/B 测试，而这对创业公司是个持续的问题：我们什么时候该开始跑 A/B 测试？你有没有一种启发式或经验法则，说“这是你真的该开始考虑跑 A/B 测试的时候”？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah, a dollar question that everybody asks. So actually, we'll put this in the notes, but I gave a talk last year, what I called it is practical defaults. And one of the things I show there is that unless you have at least tens of thousands of users, the math, the statistics just don't work out for most of the metrics that you're interested in.
turns.zh: 是的，这是个每个人都问的、价值一美元的问题。所以其实，我们会把这个放进笔记，但我去年做了一个演讲，我称之为“务实默认值”（practical defaults）。我在那里展示的一件事是：除非你至少有数万用户，否则对大多数你感兴趣的指标，那个数学、那个统计就是不成立。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: In fact, I gave an actual practical number of a retail site with some conversion rate, trying to detect changes that are at least 5% beneficial, which is something that startups should focus on. They shouldn't focus on the 1%, they should focus on the 5 and 10%. Then you need something like 200,000 users.
turns.zh: 事实上，我给出了一个实际的数字：一个有一定转化率的零售网站，试图检测至少 5% 有益的变化——那是创业公司应该聚焦的。他们不该聚焦那 1%，他们该聚焦 5% 和 10%。然后你需要大约 20 万用户。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So start experimenting when you're in the tens of thousands of users. You'll only be able to detect large effects. And then once you get to 200,000 users, then the magic starts happening. Then you can start testing a lot more. Then you have the ability to test everything and make sure that you're not degrading and getting value out of experimentation. So you ask for rule of thumb, 200,000 users, you're magical. Below that, start building the culture, start building the platform, start integrating. So that as you scale, you start to see the value.
turns.zh: 所以当你有数万用户时开始实验。你那时只能检测到大的效应。然后一旦你到了 20 万用户，魔法就开始发生了。然后你能开始测试多得多的东西。然后你就有能力测试一切，并确保你没在劣化、并从实验里获得价值。所以你问经验法则，20 万用户，你就神奇了。在那之下，开始建设文化、开始建设平台、开始整合。这样随着你规模化，你开始看到价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Love it. Coming back to this kind of concern people have of experimentation, keeps you from innovating and taking big bets, I know you have this framework overall evaluation criterion, and I think that helps with this. Can you talk a bit about that?
turns.zh: 喜欢。回到人们对实验的这个担忧——它让你没法创新和下大注，我知道你有这个总体评估标准（overall evaluation criterion）框架，而我觉得那对此有帮助。你能聊一点那个吗？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: The OEC or the overall evaluation criterion is something that I think many people that start to dabble in A/B testing miss. And the question is, what are you optimizing for? And it's a much harder question that people think because it's very easy to say we're going to optimize for money, revenue. But that's the wrong question, because you can do a lot of bad things that will improve revenue. So there has to be some countervailing metric that tells you, how do I improve revenue without hurting the user experience?
turns.zh: OEC，即总体评估标准，是我觉得很多开始涉足 A/B 测试的人会漏掉的东西。问题是，你在优化什么？而这是个比人们想的难得多的问题，因为说“我们要优化钱、收入”非常容易。但那是个错误的问题，因为你能做很多坏事来提升收入。所以必须有某个抵消性的指标告诉你：我怎么在提升收入的同时不伤害用户体验？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So let's take a good example with search. You can put more ads on a page and you will make more money. There's no doubt about it. You will make more money in the short term. The question is, what happens to the user experience, and how is that going to impact you in the long term?
turns.zh: 所以让我们拿搜索做个好例子。你能在一页上放更多广告，你就会赚更多钱。这毫无疑问。你短期内会赚更多钱。问题是，用户体验会怎样，而那长期会怎么影响你？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So we've run those experiments, and we were able to map out this number of ads causes this much increase to churn, this number of ads causes this much increase to the time that users take to find a successful result. And we came up with an OEC that is based on all these metrics that allows you to say, "Okay, I'm willing to take this additional money if I'm not hurting the user experience by more than this much." So there's a trade-off there.
turns.zh: 所以我们跑过那些实验，而我们能描画出：这个数量的广告导致这个程度的流失增加、这个数量的广告导致用户找到成功结果所花时间这个程度的增加。我们得出了一个基于所有这些指标的 OEC，让你能说“好，如果我没有把用户体验伤害超过这么多，我愿意拿这个额外的钱。”所以那里有个权衡。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: One of the nice ways to phrase this, as a constraint optimization problem. I want you to increase revenue, but I'm going to give you a fixed amount of average real estate that you can use. So for one query, you can have zero ads. For another query, you can have three ads. For a third query, you can have wider, bigger ads. I'm just going to count the pixels that you take, the vertical pixels. And I will give you some budget. And if you can under the same budget make more money, you're good to go.
turns.zh: 一个很好的表述方式，是把它当作一个约束优化问题。我想让你提升收入，但我会给你一个固定量的平均展示面积（real estate）你可以用。所以对一个查询，你可以有零个广告。对另一个查询，你可以有三个广告。对第三个查询，你可以用更宽、更大的广告。我就只算你占用的像素、垂直的像素。而我会给你某个预算。如果你能在同样的预算下赚更多钱，你就可以去做了。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So that to me turns the problem from a badly defined, let's just make more money. Any page can start plastering more ads and make more money short term, but that's not the goal. The goal is long-term growth and revenue. Then you need to insert these other criteria, and what am I doing to the user experience? One way around it is to put this constraint. Another one is just to have these other metrics. Again, something that we did, to look at the user experience. How long does it take the user to reach a successful click? What percentage of sessions are successful? These are key metrics that were part of the overall evaluation criteria, that we've used.
turns.zh: 所以那对我而言把问题从一个定义糟糕的“就让我们赚更多钱”转了过来。任何页面都能开始贴更多广告、短期赚更多钱，但那不是目标。目标是长期的增长和收入。然后你需要插入这些别的标准，而我对用户体验做了什么？绕过它的一个方式是放这个约束。另一个是就有这些别的指标。再次，我们做过的事，去看用户体验。用户到达一个成功点击要花多久？成功的 session 占百分之多少？这些是作为总体评估标准一部分的关键指标，我们用过它们。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I can give you another example by the way, from the hotel industry or Airbnb that we both worked at. You can say, "I want to improve conversion rate," but you can be smarter about it and say, "It's not just enough to convert a user to buy or to pay for a listing. I want them to be happy with it several months down the road when they actually stay there."
turns.zh: 我可以给你另一个例子，顺便，来自酒店业或我们俩都工作过的 Airbnb。你可以说“我想改善转化率”，但你可以更聪明点说“仅仅把一个用户转化去购买或为一处房源付费还不够。我要他们在几个月后实际住进去时是开心的。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So that could be part of your OEC to say, "What is the rating that they will give to that listing when they actually stay there?" And that causes an interesting problem, because you don't have this data now. You're going to have it three months from now when they actually stay. So you have to build the training set that allows you to make a prediction about whether this user, whether Lenny is going to be happy at this cheap place. Or whether no, I should offer him something more expensive, because Lenny likes to stay at nicer places where the water actually is hot and comes out of the faucet.
turns.zh: 所以那可以是你的 OEC 的一部分：说“当他们实际住进去时，他们会给那处房源什么评分？”而那造成了一个有趣的问题，因为你现在没有这个数据。你会在三个月后他们实际住进去时才有。所以你必须建立训练集，让你能预测这个用户、Lenny 会不会对这个便宜地方满意。还是说不行，我应该给他提供点更贵的，因为 Lenny 喜欢住在更好的地方、那里的水是热的、而且真的从水龙头里出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is true. Okay, so it sounds like the core to this approach is basically have a drag metric that makes sure you're not hurting something that's really important to the business, and then being very clear on what's the long-term metric we care most about.
turns.zh: 那是真的。好的，所以听起来这个 approach 的核心是基本得有个拖累性指标（drag metric），确保你没在伤害对业务真正重要的东西，然后非常清楚我们最在乎的长期指标是什么。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: To me, the key word is lifetime value, which is you have to define the OEC such that it is causally predictive of the lifetime value of the user. And that's what causes you to think about things properly, which is, am I doing something that just helps me short term, or am I doing something that will help me in the long term? Once you put that model of lifetime value, people say, "Okay, what about retention rates? We can measure that. What about the time to achieve a task? We can measure that." And those are these countervailing metrics that make the OEC useful.
turns.zh: 对我来说，关键词是终身价值（lifetime value），也就是你必须定义 OEC，使得它在因果上能预测用户的终身价值。而那正是让你正确思考事物的原因——我是在做只是帮我短期的事，还是我在做会帮我长期的事？一旦你放上那个终身价值的模型，人们会说“好，留存率呢？我们能测。完成任务的时间呢？我们能测。”而那些就是让 OEC 有用的抵消性指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And to understand these longer term metrics, what I'm hearing is use models, and forecast, and predictions, or would you suggest sometimes use a long-term holdout or some other approach? What do you find is the best way to see these long term?
turns.zh: 而要理解这些更长期的指标，我听到的是用模型、和预测和预报，还是你会建议有时用长期保留组（holdout）或别的什么方式？你发现看这些长期的最好方式是什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah, so there's two ways that I like to think about it. One is you can run long-term experiments for the goal of learning something. So I mentioned that at Bing, we did run these experiments where we increased the ads and decreased the ads, so that we will understand what happens to key metrics.
turns.zh: 是的，所以有两种方式我喜欢去想它。一个是你可以为了学习某件事的目的跑长期实验。所以我提到在 Bing，我们确实跑了这些增广告、减广告的实验，这样我们能理解关键指标会发生什么。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: The other thing is you can just build models that use some of our background knowledge or use some data science to look at historical... I'll give you another good example of this. When I came to Amazon, one of the teams that reported to me was the email team that it was not the transactional emails when you buy something, you get an email. But it was the team that sent these recommendations. "Here's a book by an author that you bought. Here's a product that we recommend." And the question is, how do we give credit to that team?
turns.zh: 另一件事是你可以就建模型，用我们的一些背景知识或一些数据科学去看历史的……我给你另一个好例子。当我到 Amazon 时，汇报给我的团队之一是邮件团队——不是你买东西时那种交易邮件，你收到一封邮件。而是发这些推荐信的团队。“这是你买过的作者的书。这是我们推荐的产品。”而问题是，我们怎么给那个团队记功？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And the initial version was, whenever a user comes from the email and purchases something on Amazon, we're going to give that email credit. Well, it turned out this had no countervailing metric. The more emails you send, the more money you're going to credit the team. And so that led to spam. Literally a really interesting problem. The team just ramped up the number of emails that they were sending out, and claimed to make more money, and their fitness function improved.
turns.zh: 而最初版本是，每当一个用户从邮件来、并在 Amazon 买了东西，我们就给那封邮件记功。嗯，结果这没有任何抵消性指标。你发的邮件越多，你给团队记的功就越多。而那导致了垃圾邮件。真的个很有趣的问题。团队就拉高了他们发出的邮件数量，声称赚了更多钱，而他们的适应度函数（fitness function）改善了。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So then we backed up and then we said, "Okay, we can either phrase this as a constraint satisfaction problem. You're allowed to send user an email every X days or," which is what we ended up doing is, "Let's model the cost of spamming the users."
turns.zh: 所以然后我们退回来，然后我们说“好，我们可以要么把它表述为一个约束满足问题。你被允许每 X 天给用户发一封邮件”，或者——而我们最后做的是——我们建模骚扰用户的成本。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: What's that cost? Well, when they unsubscribe, we can't mail them. So we did some data science study on the side and we said, "What is the value that we're losing from an unsubscribe?" And we came up with a number, it was a few dollars. But the point was, now we have this countervailing metric. We say, "Here's the money that we generate from the emails. Here's the money that we're losing on long-term value. What's the trade-off?" And then when we started to incorporate those formula, more than half the campaigns that were being sent were negative.
turns.zh: 那个成本是什么？嗯，当他们退订时，我们就不能给他们发邮件了。所以我们侧面做了些数据科学研究，说“我们从一个退订上损失的价值是什么？”我们得出了一个数字，是几美元。但重点是，现在我们有了这个抵消性指标。我们说“这是我们从邮件产生的钱。这是我们在长期价值上损失的钱。权衡是什么？”而当我们开始把那些公式纳入，正在发送的 campaign 中超过一半是负面的。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So it was a huge insight at Amazon about how to send the right campaigns. And this is what I like about these discoveries. This fact that we integrated the unsubscribe led us to a new feature to say, "Well, let's not lose their future lifetime value through email. When they unsubscribe, let's offer them by default to unsubscribe from this campaign."
turns.zh: 所以那是在 Amazon 关于怎么发正确 campaign 的一个巨大洞见。而这正是我喜欢这些发现的原因。我们把退订整合进去这个事实，引出了一个功能：“好吧，别通过邮件失去他们未来的终身价值。当他们退订时，让我们默认提供让他们退订这个 campaign。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So when you get an email, there's a new book by the author. The default to unsubscribe would be unsubscribe me from author emails. And so now, the negative, the countervailing metric is much smaller. And so again, this was a breakthrough in our ability to send more emails, and understand based on what users were unsubscribing from, which ones are really beneficial.
turns.zh: 所以当你收到一封邮件，说某作者有新书。默认退订会是“退订作者的邮件”。而现在，那个负面、那个抵消性指标就小得多了。而再次，这是我们能发更多邮件、并基于用户退订了什么来理解哪些真的有益的突破。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the surprising results.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这些令人惊讶的结果。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: We all love them. This is the humbling reality. And people talk about the fact that A/B testing sometimes leads you to incremental... I actually think that many of these small insights lead to fundamental insights about which areas to go, some strategies we should take, some things we should develop. Helps a lot.
turns.zh: 我们都爱它们。这是让人谦卑的现实。而人们谈论 A/B 测试有时把你引向增量……我其实觉得很多这些小洞见引向关于该去哪些领域、我们该采取哪些策略、我们该开发哪些东西的基本洞见。帮了大忙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This makes me think about how every time I've done a full redesign of a product, I don't think ever, has it ever been a positive result. And then the team always ends up having to claw back what they just hurt and try to figure out what they messed up. Is that your experience too?
turns.zh: 这让我想到，每次我做产品的完整重设计，我不觉得有过一次是正面的结果。然后团队总是得去把刚伤害的东西 claw back、并试图搞清楚他们搞砸了什么。那也是你的经验吗？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Absolutely, yeah. In fact, I've published some of these in LinkedIn posts showing a large set of big launches and redesigns that dramatically failed, and it happens very often. So the right way to do this is to say, "Yes, we want to do a redesign, but let's do it in steps and test on the way and adjust," so you don't need to take 17 new changes, that many of them are going to fail. Start to move incrementally in a direction that you believe is beneficial. Adjust on the way.
turns.zh: 绝对，是的。事实上，我在 LinkedIn 帖子发过一些，展示一大组大幅失败的大发布和重设计，而它发生得非常频繁。所以做这个的正确方式是说“是的，我们想做重设计，但让我们分步做、并在过程中测试和调整”，这样你不用一次拿 17 个新改动、其中很多会失败。朝着你相信有益的方向，增量地开始移动。在过程中调整。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The worst part of those experiences I find is it took three to six months to build it. And by the time it's launched, it's just like, "We're not going to unlaunch this. Everyone's been working in this direction. All the new features are assuming this is going to work," and you're basically stuck.
turns.zh: 我发现那些经历最糟的部分是，它花了三到六个月去建。而到它发布时，就像“我们不打算取消发布了。每个人都在朝这个方向工作。所有新功能都假设这会奏效”，而你基本被困住了。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I mean, this is a sunk cost fallacy. We invested so many years in it. Let's launch this, even though it's bad for the user. No, that's terrible. Yeah. Yeah. So this is the other advantage of recognizing this humble reality that most ideas fail. If you believe in that statistics that I published, then doing 17 changes together is more likely to be negative. Do them in smaller increments, learn from, it's called OFAT one-factor-at-a-time. Do one factor, learn from it, and adjust. Of the 17, maybe you have four good ideas. Those are the ones that will launch and be positive.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这是沉没成本谬误。我们在这上面投了好多年。让我们发布这个，即使它对用户不好。不，那很糟。是的。是的。所以这是认识到这个谦卑现实的另一个好处——大多数想法会失败。如果你相信我发表的那个统计，那么把 17 个改动一起做更可能是负面的。把它们做成更小的增量，从中学习，这叫 OFAT，一次一个因素（one-factor-at-a-time）。做一个因素，从中学习，然后调整。那 17 个里，也许你有四个好想法。那些才是会上线、会是正面的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I generally agree with that, and always try to avoid a big redesign, but it's hard to avoid them completely. There's often team members that are really passionate like, "We just need to rethink this whole experience. We're not going to incrementally get there." Have you found anything effective in helping people either see this perspective, or just making a larger bet more successful?
turns.zh: 我大体同意那个，并且总是试图避免大重设计，但完全避免它们很难。经常有团队成员真的很有热情，像“我们就是需要重新思考整个体验。我们不会增量地到达那里。”你有没有发现什么有效的方法，去帮助人们要么看到这个视角，要么就是让一个更大的赌注更成功？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: By the way, I'm not opposed to large redesigns. I try to give the team the data to say, "Look, here are lots of examples where big redesigns fail." Try to decompose your redesign if you can't decompose it to one factor at a time, to a small set of factors at a time. And learn from these smaller changes what works and what doesn't.
turns.zh: 顺便，我不反对大重设计。我试着给团队数据说“看，这里有很多大重设计失败的例子。”试着把你的重设计分解——如果你不能一次分解到一个因素，就一次到一小批因素。并从这些更小的改动里学习什么有效、什么无效。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Now, it's also possible to do a complete redesign. Just, as you said yourself, be ready to fail. I mean, do you really want to work on something for six months or a year, and then run the A/B test, and realize that you've hurt revenues or other key metrics by several percentage points? And a data-driven organization will not allow you to launch. What are you going to write in your annual review?
turns.zh: 现在，做一个完整的重设计也是可能的。只是，正如你自己说的，准备好失败。我的意思是，你真的想为某件事工作六个月或一年，然后跑 A/B 测试，然后意识到你把收入或其他关键指标伤了几个百分点？而一个数据驱动的组织不会允许你发布。你要在你的年度评估里写什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But nobody ever thinks it's going to fail. They think, "No, we got this. We've talked to so many people."
turns.zh: 但没人会觉得它会失败。他们想“不，我们搞定了。我们和这么多人聊过了。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: But I think organizations that start to run experiments are humbled early on from the smaller changes. Right? You're right. I'll tell you a funny story. When I came from Amazon to Microsoft, I joined the group, and for one reason or another, that group disbanded a month after I joined.
turns.zh: 但我觉得开始跑实验的组织，会早早地在更小的改动上变得谦卑。对吧？你是对的。我给你讲个好笑的故事。当我从 Amazon 到 Microsoft，我加入了那个组，而出于某种原因，那个组在我加入一个月后就解散了。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And so people came to me and said, "Look, you just joined the company. You're at partner level. You figure out how you can help Microsoft." And I said, "I'm going to build an experimentation platform," because nobody at Microsoft is running experiments. And more than 50% of ideas in Amazon that we tried failed. And the classical response was, "We have better PMs here."
turns.zh: 所以人们来找我说“看，你刚加入公司。你是 partner 级别。你想想怎么帮 Microsoft。”而我说“我要建一个实验平台”，因为 Microsoft 没人在跑实验。而我们在 Amazon 试的想法里超过 50% 失败了。而经典的反应是“我们这儿的 PM 更好。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Right? There was this complete denial that it's possible that 50% of ideas that Microsoft is implementing, in a three-year development cycle by the way. This is how long it took Office to release. It was a classical every three years we release.
turns.zh: 对吧？有一种完全的否认，认为 Microsoft 正在实现的想法有 50% 可能失败——顺便，那是个三年的开发周期。这是 Office 发布要花的时间。经典的是每三年我们发布一次。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And the data came about showing that Bing was the first to truly implement experimentation at scale. And we shared with the rest of the companies the surprising results. And so when Office was... And this was credit to Qi Lu and Satya Nadella, they were ones that says, "Ronny, you try to get Office to run experiments. We'll give you the air support." And it was hard, but we did it. It took a while, but Office started to run experiments, and they realized that many of their ideas are failing.
turns.zh: 而数据表明 Bing 是第一个真正在规模上实现实验的。而我们把那些令人惊讶的结果分享给公司的其他部门。所以当 Office 时……而这要归功于 Qi Lu 和 Satya Nadella，他们是说“Ronny，你试着让 Office 跑实验。我们给你空中支援。”而那很难，但我们做到了。花了阵子，但 Office 开始跑实验，而他们意识到他们的很多想法在失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that there's a site of a failed redesigns. Is that in your book or is that a site that you can point people to, to help build this case?
turns.zh: 你说有个失败重设计的网站。那是在你的书里，还是个你能指给人们、帮助建立这个 case 的网站？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I teach this in my class, but I think I've posted this on LinkedIn and answered some questions. I'm happy to put that in the notes.
turns.zh: 我在课上教这个，但我觉得我在 LinkedIn 发过这个、并回答过一些问题。我很乐意把它放进笔记。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. We'll put that in the show notes. Because I think that's the kind of data that often helps convince a team, "Maybe we shouldn't rethink this entire onboarding flow from scratch. Maybe we should iterate towards and learn as we go."
turns.zh: 好的，酷。我们会把它放进节目笔记。因为我觉得那种数据常常有助于说服一个团队“也许我们不该从零重新思考整个 onboarding 流程。也许我们应该边迭代边学。”

turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Eppo. Eppo is a next generation A/B testing platform built by Airbnb alums for modern growth teams. Companies like DraftKings, Zapier, ClickUp, Twitch, and Cameo rely on Eppo to power their experiments.
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Eppo 赞助。Eppo 是一个下一代 A/B 测试平台，由 Airbnb 校友为现代增长团队打造。DraftKings、Zapier、ClickUp、Twitch 和 Cameo 等公司依赖 Eppo 来驱动他们的实验。

turns.en: Wherever you work, running experiments is increasingly essential, but there are no commercial tools that integrate with a modern growth team stack. This leads to wasted time building internal tools or trying to run your own experiments through a clunky marketing tool.
turns.zh: 无论你在哪工作，跑实验都越来越重要，但没有能整合现代增长团队技术栈的商业工具。这导致浪费时间建内部工具，或试图通过一个笨重的营销工具来跑你自己的实验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I was at Airbnb, one of the things that I loved most about working there was our experimentation platform, where I was able to slice and dice data by device types, country, user stage.
turns.zh: 当我在 Airbnb 时，我在那里工作最爱的事之一，就是我们的实验平台，在那里我能按设备类型、国家、用户阶段来切分和剖析数据。
