Eppo supports tests on the front end, on the back end, email marketing, even machine learning clients. Check out Eppo at geteppo.com, that's geteppo.com, and 10X your experiment velocity.
turns.zh: Eppo 做到所有这些以及更多，快速交付结果，避免恼人的冗长分析周期，并帮你轻松找到你发现的任何问题的根本原因。Eppo 让你超越基础的点击通过指标，而是用你的北极星指标如激活、留存、订阅和支付。Eppo 支持前端、后端、邮件营销、甚至机器学习客户端的测试。在 geteppo.com 看看 Eppo，就是 geteppo.com，让你的实验速度 10 倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is it ever worth just going, "Let's just rethink this whole thing and just give it a shot," to break out of a local minima or local maxima essentially?
turns.zh: 有没有时候值得就“让我们重新思考整个东西、就试一把”，来本质上打破局部极小值或局部极大值？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah. So I think what you said is fair. I do want to allocate some percentage of resources to big bets. As you said, we've been optimizing this thing to hell. Could we completely redesign it? It's a very valid idea. You may be able to break out of a local minima. What I'm telling you is 80% of the time, you will fail. So be ready for that. What people usually expect is, "My redesign is going to work." No, you're most likely going to fail, but if you do succeed, it's a breakthrough.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我觉得你说的公平。我确实想把一定百分比的资源分配到大的赌注上。正如你说的，我们已经把这个东西优化到 hell 了。我们能完全重设计它吗？这是个非常有效的想法。你可能能打破一个局部极小。我告诉你的是，80% 的时候，你会失败。所以为此准备好。人们通常预期的是“我的重设计会奏效。”不，你最可能失败，但如果你成功了，那是个突破。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like this 80% rule of thumb. Is that just a simple way of thinking about it? 80% of your-
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个 80% 的经验法则。那只是个思考它的简单方式吗？80% 你的——

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: That's my rule of thumb. And I've heard people say it's 70% or 80%. But it's in that area where I think when you talk about how much to invest in the known versus the high risk, high reward, that's usually the right percentage that most organizations end up doing this allocation, right? You interviewed Shreyas. I think he mentioned that Google is like 70% the searching ads, and it's 20% for some of the apps and new stuff, and then it's the 10% for infrastructure.
turns.zh: 那是我的经验法则。而我听过人们说它是 70% 或 80%。但它就在那个区域——我觉得当你聊在已知的 vs 高风险高回报之间投多少时，那通常是大多数组织最终做这个分配的正确百分比，对吧？你采访过 Shreyas。我觉得他提到 Google 是 70% 搜索广告、20% 给一些应用和新东西、然后 10% 给基础设施。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think the most important point there is if you're not running an experiment, 70% of stuff you're shipping is hurting your business.
turns.zh: 而我觉得那里最重要的一点是：如果你不在跑实验，你发布的 70% 的东西在伤害你的业务。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Well, it's not hurting, it's flat too negative. Some of them are flat. And by the way, flat to me, if something is not Statsig, that's a no ship, because you've just introduced more code. There is a maintenance overhead to shipping your stuff. I've heard people say, "Look, we already spent all this time. The team will be demotivated if we don't ship it." And I'm, "No, that's wrong guys. Let's make sure that we understand that shipping this project has no value, is complicating the code base. Maintenance costs will go up." You don't ship on flat, unless it's a legal requirement. When legal comes along and says, "You have to do X or Y," you have to ship on flat or even negative. And that's understandable.
turns.zh: 嗯，不是伤害，是持平到负面。有些是持平的。顺便，持平对我来说，如果某物不是 Statsig 显著，那是不发布（no ship），因为你刚引入了更多代码。发布你的东西有维护开销。我听过人们说“看，我们已经花了所有这些时间。如果我们不发布，团队会丧失动力。”而我“不，那错了兄弟们。让我们确保我们理解发布这个项目没有价值，是在把代码库复杂化。维护成本会上升。”你不在持平上发布，除非是法律要求。当法律找来、说“你必须做 X 或 Y”，你不得不在持平甚至负面上发布。而那可以理解。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: But again, I think that's something that a lot of people make the mistake of saying, "Legal told us we have to do this, therefore we're going to take the hits." No, legal gave you a framework that you have to work under. Try three different things, and ship the one that hurts the least.
turns.zh: 但再次，我觉得那是很多人犯错误说的“法律告诉我们必须做这个，因此我们要承受这些打击。”不，法律给了你一个你必须在之下工作的框架。试三种不同的东西，然后发布伤害最小的那一个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me when Airbnb launched the rebrand, even that they ran as an experiment with the entire homepage redesigned, the new logo, and all that. And I think there was a long-term holdout even, and I think it was positive in the end from what I remember.
turns.zh: 那让我想起 Airbnb 发布品牌重塑时，连那个他们也是作为实验跑的——整个首页重设计、新 logo、等等。而我觉得甚至有个长期保留组（holdout），而我想最后从我记得是正向的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of Airbnb, I want to chat about Airbnb briefly. I know you're limited in what you can share, but it's interesting that Airbnb seems to be moving in this other direction where it's becoming a lot more top-down, Brian vision oriented. And Brian's even talked about how he's less motivated to run experiments. He doesn't want to run as many experiments as they used to. Things are going well, and so it's hard to argue with the success potentially. You worked there for many years. You ran the search team essentially. I guess, what was your experience like there? And then roughly, what's your sense of how things are going, where it's going?
turns.zh: 说到 Airbnb，我想简单聊聊 Airbnb。我知道你在能分享什么上是受限的，但有趣的是 Airbnb 似乎在往另一个方向移动——变得更自上而下、Brian 愿景导向。而 Brian 甚至谈到他跑实验的动力更低。他不想像以前那样跑那么多实验。事情进展得不错，所以很难去反驳那种成功的可能性。你在那工作了很多年。你本质上领导了搜索团队。我想，你那的经历是怎样的？然后大致上，你对事情进展如何、往哪去，有什么感觉？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Well as you know, I'm restricted from talking about Airbnb. I will say a few things that I am allowed to say. One is in my team in search relevance, everything was A/B tested. So while Brian can focus on some of the design aspects, the people who are actually doing the neural networks and the search, everything was A/B tested to hell. So nothing was launching without an A/B test. We had targets around improving certain metrics, and everything was done A/B test.
turns.zh: 如你所知，我被限制不能谈 Airbnb。我会说几件我可以说的事。一个是在我搜索相关性的团队，一切都被 A/B 测试了。所以虽然 Brian 能聚焦在一些设计方面，真正做神经网络和搜索的人，一切都被 A/B 测试到 hell。所以没有 A/B 测试就没有东西上线。我们有围绕改善某些指标的目标，而一切都是 A/B 测试做的。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Now other teams, some did, some did not. I will say that when you say things are going well, I think we don't know the counterfactual. I believe that had Airbnb kept people like Greg Greeley, which was pushing for a lot more data driven, and had Airbnb run more experiments, it would've been in a better state than today. But it's the counterfactual. We don't know.
turns.zh: 现在别的团队，有的做了，有的没做。我会说当你说事情进展得不错，我觉得我们不知道反事实（counterfactual）。我相信如果 Airbnb 留住了像 Greg Greeley 这样的人——他推动更多的数据驱动——并且如果 Airbnb 跑了更多实验，它会比今天状态更好。但那是反事实。我们不知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really interesting perspective. Airbnb's such an interesting natural experiment of a way of doing things differently. There's de-emphasizing experiments, and also, they turned off paid ads during Covid. And I don't know where it is now, but it feels like it's become a much smaller part of the growth strategy. Who knows if they've ramped it up to back to where it's today, but I think it's going to be a really interesting case study looking back five, 10 years from now.
turns.zh: 那是个很有趣的视角。Airbnb 是个很有趣的自然实验——一种不同的做事方式。它弱化了实验，而且，他们在 Covid 期间关掉了付费广告。我不知道它现在到哪了，但感觉它成了增长策略里小得多的部分。谁知道他们有没有把它加回今天这样的水平，但我觉得回头看五年、十年后，它会是个真的有趣的案例研究。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: It's a one-off experiment where it's hard to assign value to some of the things that Airbnb is doing. I personally believe it could have been a lot bigger and a lot more successful if it had run more controlled experiments. But I can't speak about some of those that I ran and that showed that some of the things that were initially untested were actually negative and could be better.
turns.zh: 它是个一次性的实验，很难给 Airbnb 正在做的某些东西赋价值。我个人相信如果它跑了更多受控实验，它本可以大得多、成功得多。但我不能谈我跑过的其中一些、那些显示出一些最初没测试的其实是负面的、并且可以更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Mysterious. One more question. Airbnb, you were there during Covid, which was quite a wild time for Airbnb. We had Sanchan on the podcast talking about all the craziness that went on when travel basically stopped, and there was a sense that Airbnb was done, and travel's not going to happen for years and years. What's your take on experimentation in that world where you have to really move fast, make crazy decisions, and make big decisions? What was it like during that time?
turns.zh: 好。神秘。再一个问题。Airbnb，你在 Covid 期间在那里，那对 Airbnb 是相当疯狂的时期。我们请了 Sanchan 上播客，聊旅行基本停摆时发生的所有疯狂，而有一种感觉是 Airbnb 完了，旅行好多年都不会发生。你对那个世界里实验的看法是怎样的——你真的得快速移动、做疯狂的决定、做大决定？那段时间是什么样？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So I think actually in a state like that, it's even more important to run A/B tests, right? Because what you want to be able to see is if we're making this change, is it actually helping in the current environment? There's this idea of external generalizability. Is it going to work out now during Covid? Is it going to generalize later on? These are things that you can really answer with the controlled experiments, and sometimes it means that you might have to replicate them six months down when Covid say is not as impactful as it is.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得其实在那样一种状态下，跑 A/B 测试更重要，对吧？因为你想要能看到的是：如果我们做这个改动，它在当前环境里真的有帮助吗？有个外部可泛化性（external generalizability）的想法。它在 Covid 期间现在会奏效吗？它之后会泛化吗？这些是你能用受控实验真正回答的东西，而有时那意味着你可能得在六个月后 Covid 没那么有影响时重复它们。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Saying that you have to make decisions quickly, to me, I'll point you to the success rate. If in peace time you're wrong two thirds to 80% of the time, why would you be subtly right in wartime, in Covid time?
turns.zh: 说你必须快速做决定，对我而言，我会指向那个成功率。如果在和平时期你有三分之二到 80% 的时间是错的，为什么你在战时、在 Covid 时期会突然是对的？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So I don't believe in the idea that because bookings went down materially, the company should suddenly not be data driven and do things differently. I think if Airbnb stayed the course, did nothing, the revenue would've gone up in the same way.
turns.zh: 所以我不相信那种想法：因为预订量大幅下降了，公司就该突然不数据驱动、用不同方式做事。我觉得如果 Airbnb 按原路线走、什么都不做，收入会以同样的方式上去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating.
turns.zh: 迷人。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: In fact, if you look at one investment, one big investment that was done at the time was online experiences, and the initial data wasn't very promising. And I think today, it's a footnote.
turns.zh: 事实上，如果你看一个投资、当时做的一个大投资，是在线体验（online experiences），而最初的数据不是很有希望。而我觉得今天，它只是个脚注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Another case study for the history books, Airbnb experiences. I want to shift a little bit and talk about your book, which you mentioned a couple times. It's called Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments, and I think it's basically the book on A/B testing. Let me ask you, what surprised you most about writing this book, and putting it out, and the reaction to it?
turns.zh: 是的。另一个留给史册的案例研究，Airbnb experiences。我想稍微转个向，聊聊你的书，你提过几次。它叫《Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments（可信赖的在线受控实验）》，而我觉得它基本就是关于 A/B 测试的那本书。让我问你，写这本书、把它推出、以及它的反响，什么最让你惊讶？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I was pleasantly surprised that it sold more than what we thought, more than what Cambridge predicted. So when first we were approached by Cambridge after a tutorial that we did to write a book, I was like, "I don't know, this is too small of a niche area."
turns.zh: 我惊喜地发现它卖得比我们想的、比 Cambridge 预测的都多。所以当我们做了一个教程后被 Cambridge 找去写书，我就像“我不知道，这是个太小的细分领域。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And they were saying, "So you'll be able to sell a few thousand copies and help the world." And I found my co-authors, which are great. And we wrote a book that we thought is not statistically oriented, has fewer formulas than you normally see, and focuses on the practical aspects and on trust, which is the key.
turns.zh: 而他们说“所以你能卖几千本，并帮助世界。”而我找到了我的合著者，都很棒。我们写了本书，我们认为它不是统计导向的，公式比你通常看到的少，并聚焦于实践方面和信任——那是关键。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: The book, as I said, was more successful. It sold over 20,000 copies in English. It was translated to Chinese, Korean, Japanese, and Russian. And so it's great to see that we help the world become more data-driven with experimentation, and I'm happy because of that. I was pleasantly surprised.
turns.zh: 如我所说，这本书更成功。英文版卖了超过 2 万本。它被译成了中文、韩文、日文和俄文。所以看到我们帮助世界通过实验变得更数据驱动，很棒，而我因此高兴。我惊喜了。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: By the way, all proceeds from the book are donated to charity. So if I'm pitching the book here, there is no financial gain for me from having more copies sold. I think we made that decision, which was a good decision. All proceeds go with the charity.
turns.zh: 顺便，这本书的所有收益都捐给了慈善。所以如果我在这里推销书，卖更多本对我没有任何经济收益。我觉得我们做了那个决定，是个好决定。所有收益都归慈善。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I didn't know that. We'll link to the book in the show notes. Trust is in the title. You just mentioned how important trust is to experimentation. A lot of people talk about, "How do I run experiments faster?" You focus a lot on trust. Why is trust so important in running experiments?
turns.zh: 惊人。我不知道那个。我们会在节目笔记里放这本书的链接。信赖（Trust）在标题里。你刚提到信任对实验多重要。很多人聊“我怎么更快跑实验？”你大量聚焦在信任上。为什么信任在跑实验时这么重要？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So to me, the experimentation platform is the safety net, and it's an oracle. So it serves really two purposes. The safety net means that if you launch something bad, you should be able to abort quickly, right? Safe deployments, safe velocity. There's some names for this. But this is one key value that the platform can give you.
turns.zh: 所以对我来说，实验平台是安全网，也是神谕。所以它真正服务于两个目的。安全网意味着如果你发布了糟糕的东西，你应该能快速中止，对吧？安全部署、安全速度。有一些名字给这个。但这是平台能给你的一个关键价值。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: The other one, which is the more standard one, is at the end of the two-week experiment, we will tell you what happened to your key metric and to many of the other surrogate, and debugging, and guardrail metrics. Trust builds up, it's easy to lose.
turns.zh: 另一个，更标准的那个，是在两周实验结束时，我们会告诉你你的关键指标、以及许多其他的代理指标、调试指标和护栏指标发生了什么。信任建立起来，却很容易失去。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And so to me, it is very important that when you present this and say, "This is science, this is a controlled experiment, this is the resolve," you better believe that this is trustworthy.
turns.zh: 所以对我来说，非常重要的一点是，当你展示这个并说“这是科学，这是受控实验，这是结论”时，你最好相信这是可信赖的。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And so I focus on that a lot. I think it allowed us to gain the organizational trust that this is really... And the nice thing is when we built all this checks to make sure that the experiment is correct, if there were something wrong with it, we would stop and say, "Hey, something is wrong with the experiment."
turns.zh: 所以我大量聚焦在那个上。我觉得它让我们获得了组织的信任，相信这真的是……而好的是，当我们建了所有这些检查来确保实验正确时，如果它有什么问题，我们会停下来并说“嘿，实验有哪里不对。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And I think that's something that some of the early implementations in other places did not do, and it was a big mistake. I've mentioned this in my book so I can mention this here.
turns.zh: 而我觉得那是一些其他地方早期实现没做的，而那是个大错误。我在我的书里提过，所以我可以在这里提。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Optimizely in its early days were very statistically naive. They sort of said, "Hey, we're real time. We can compute your P values in real time," and then you can stop an experiment when the P value is statistically significant. That is a big mistake. That inflates your, what's called type one error or the false positive rate materially. So if you think you've got a 5% type one error, or you aim for that P value less than 0.05, using real time P value monitoring to optimize the offer, you would probably have a 30% error rate.
turns.zh: Optimizely 在早期非常缺乏统计素养。他们有点像说“嘿，我们是实时的。我们能实时计算你的 P 值”，然后你可以在 P 值统计显著时停止一个实验。那是个大错误。那会实质性地推高你的所谓一类错误（type one error）或假阳性率。所以如果你以为你有一个 5% 的一类错误，或者你瞄准那个 P 值小于 0.05，用实时监控 P 值来优化那个 offer，你大概会有 30% 的错误率。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So what this led is that people that started using Optimizely thought that the platform was telling them they were very successful. But when they actually started to see, "Well it told us this is positive revenue, but I don't see this over time. By now, we should have made double the money."
turns.zh: 所以这导致那些开始用 Optimizely 的人以为平台在告诉他们非常成功。但当他们实际开始看到“嗯，它告诉我们这是正向收入，但我一段时间没看到这个。到现在，我们应该已经赚了一倍的钱了。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So their questions started to come up around the trust in the platform. There's a very famous post that somebody wrote about how, "Optimizely almost got me fired," by a person who basically said, "Look, I came to the org. I said, 'We have all these successes.' But then I said, 'Something is wrong.'"
turns.zh: 所以他们对平台的信任开始出问题。有个非常著名的帖子，某人写道“Optimizely 差点让我被炒了”，由一个人写的，他基本说“看，我来到这个组织。我说‘我们有所有这些成功’。但然后我说‘哪里不对。’”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And he tells of how he ran an A/A test when there is no difference between the A and the B. And Optimizely told him that it was statistically significant too many times. Optimizely learned. Optimizely, several people pointed, I pointed this out in my Amazon review of the book that the authors wrote early on. I said, "Hey, you're not doing the statistics correctly."
turns.zh: 而他讲述了他是怎么跑了一个 A/A 测试——A 和 B 之间没有区别。而 Optimizely 告诉他太多次它是统计显著的。Optimizely 学到了。Optimizely，几个人指出，我在我对作者早期写的书的 Amazon 评论里指出了这个。我说“嘿，你们统计没做对。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Ramesh Johari at Stanford pointed this out, became a consultant to the company, and then they fixed it. But to me, that's a very good example of how to lose trust. They lost a lot of trust in the market. They lost all this trust because they built something that had very much inflated error rate.
turns.zh: Stanford 的 Ramesh Johari 指出了这个，成了公司的顾问，然后他们修好了它。但对我而言，那是个很好的如何失去信任的例子。他们在市场上失去了很多信任。他们失去所有这些信任，因为他们建了某种有非常被推高的错误率的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is pretty scary to think about you've been running all these experiments, and they weren't actually telling you accurate results. What are signs that what you're doing may not be valid if you're starting to run experiments? And then how do you avoid having that situation? What kind of tips can you share for people trying to run experiments?
turns.zh: 想到你一直在跑所有这些实验、而它们其实没在告诉你准确结果，挺吓人的。如果你开始跑实验，有什么迹象表明你做的事情可能无效？然后你怎么避免那种情况？你能给想跑实验的人什么建议？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: There's a whole chapter of that in my book, but I'll say one of the things that is the most common occurrence by far, which is a sample ratio mismatch. Now, what is a sample ratio mismatch?
turns.zh: 我的书里有一整章讲那个，但我会说到目前为止最常见的发生的事之一，是样本比例失配（sample ratio mismatch）。现在，什么是样本比例失配？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: If you design the experiment to send 50% of users to control and 50% of users to treatment, it's supposed to be a random number, or a hash function. If you get something off from 50%, it's a red flag.
turns.zh: 如果你设计实验把 50% 的用户送到对照组（control）、50% 送到处理组（treatment），它本该是个随机数，或哈希函数。如果你得到的偏离 50%，那是个红旗。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So let's take a real example. Let's say you're running an experiment, and it's large, it's got a million users, and you've got 50.2. So people say, "Well, I don't know. It's not going to be exactly the same as 50.2. Reasonable or not?" Well, there's a formula that you can plug in. I have a spreadsheet available for those that are interested, and you can tell, here's how many users are in control. Here's how many users have in treatment. My design was 50/50, and it tells you the probability that this could have happened by chance.
turns.zh: 所以让我们拿个真实例子。假设你跑一个实验，它很大，有一百万用户，而你得到的是 50.2。所以人们说“嗯，我不知道。它不会正好和 50.2 一样。合理还是不合理？”嗯，有个公式你能代入。我有个表格给那些感兴趣的，而你能告诉，这里有这么多个用户在对照组。这里有这么多个在处理组。我的设计是 50/50，而它告诉你这个能偶然发生的概率。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Now in a case like this, you plug in the numbers, it might tell you that this should happen one in half a million experiments. Well, unless you've run half a million experiment, very unlikely that you would get a 50.2 versus 49.8 split. And therefore, something is wrong with the experiment.
turns.zh: 现在在这种 case，你代入数字，它可能会告诉你这应该每五十万个实验才发生一次。嗯，除非你跑了五十万个实验，你得到 50.2 vs 49.8 的分配非常不可能。因此，实验哪里不对。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I remember when we implemented this check, we were surprised to see how many experiments suffered from this. Right? And there's a paper that was published, 2018, where we share that at Microsoft, even though we'd be running experiments for a while, is around 8% of experiments that suffered from the sample ratio mismatch.
turns.zh: 我记得当我们实现这个检查时，我们惊讶地看到有多少实验受这个困扰。对吧？而有篇 2018 年发表的论文，我们分享说在微软，即使我们已经跑实验一阵了，大约有 8% 的实验受样本比例失配困扰。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And it's a big number. I think about this. You're running 20,000 experiments a year. So many of them, 8% of them are invalid. And somebody has to go down and understand, what happened here? We know that we can't trust the results, but why?
turns.zh: 而那是个大数字。我想想这个。你一年跑 2 万个实验。所以很多，8% 的它们无效。而有人得下去理解，这里发生了什么？我们知道我们不能信任结果，但为什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So over time, you begin to understand there's something wrong with the data pipeline. There's something that happens with bots. Bots are a very common factor for causing sample ratio mismatch. So that paper that was published by my team talks about how to diagnose sample ratio mismatches.
turns.zh: 所以随着时间，你开始理解数据流水线哪里不对。机器人（bots）是个非常常见的造成样本比例失配的因素。所以那篇我团队发表的论文谈了怎么诊断样本比例失配。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: In the last probably year and a half, it was amazing to see all these third party companies implement sample ratio mismatches, and all of them were reporting, "Oh my god, 6%, 8%, 10%." So it's sometimes fun to go back and say, how many of your results in the past were invalid before you had this sample ratio mismatched test?
turns.zh: 在大概去年这一年半里，看到所有这些第三方公司实现样本比例失配、而全都报告“我的天，6%、8%、10%”，很惊人。所以有时回去说，在你们有这个样本比例失配测试之前，你们过去有多少结果是无效的，挺好玩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's frightening. Is the most common reason this happens is you're assigning users in the wrong place in your code?
turns.zh: 是的，那吓人。发生这个最常见的原因是你在代码里错误的地方分配了用户吗？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So when you say most common, I think the most common is bots. Somehow, they hit the controller, the treatment in different proportions. Because you change the website, the bot may fail to parse the page, and try to hit it more often. And that's a classical example. Another one is just the data pipeline.
turns.zh: 所以当你说最常见，我觉得最常见的是 bots。它们不知怎的以不同比例打到 controller、treatment。因为你改了网站，bot 可能没法解析页面，并试图更频繁地打它。而那是经典例子。另一个就只是数据流水线。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: We've had cases where we were trying to remove bad traffic under certain conditions, and it was skewed because of the control and treatment. I've seen people that start an experiment in the middle of the site on some page, but they don't realize that some campaign is pushing people from the side.
turns.zh: 我们有过这种情况：我们在某些条件下试图移除坏流量，而它因为对照组和处理组而偏斜了。我见过人们在网站中间某个页面启动一个实验，但他们没意识到某个 campaign 正从侧面推人。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So there's multiple reasons. It is surprising how often this happens. And I'll tell you a funny story, which is when we first added this test to the platform, we just put a banner say, "You have a sample ratio mismatch. Do not trust these results." And we noticed that people ignored it. They were starting to present results that had this banner.
turns.zh: 所以有多种原因。这发生得有多频繁令人惊讶。而我给你讲个好笑的故事，就是我们第一次把这个测试加到平台上时，我们就放了个横幅说“你有样本比例失配。不要信任这些结果。”而我们注意到人们忽略了它。他们开始展示有这个横幅的结果。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And so we blanked out the scorecard. We put a big red, "Can't see this result. You have a sample ratio mismatch. Click to expose the results." And why we do we need that okay? We need that okay button because you want to be able to debug the reasons, and sometimes the metrics help you understand why you have a sample ratio mismatch.
turns.zh: 所以我们把记分卡（scorecard）抹掉了。我们放了个大红的“看不到这个结果。你有样本比例失配。点击暴露结果。”而为什么我们需要那个 okay？我们需要那个 okay 按钮，因为你想能调试原因，而有时那些指标帮你理解你为什么有样本比例失配。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So we blanked out the scorecard, we had this button, and then we started to see that people pressed the button and still presented the results of experiments with sample ratio mismatch. And so we ended up with an amazing compromise, which is every number in the scorecard was highlighted with a red line, so that if you took a screenshot, other people could tell you how to sample ratio mismatch.
turns.zh: 所以我们抹掉了记分卡，我们有了这个按钮，然后我们开始看到人们按了按钮、却仍然展示有样本比例失配的实验的结果。所以我们最终有了一个惊人的折中，就是记分卡里的每个数字都用一条红线高亮，这样如果你截了图，别人能告诉你这是样本比例失配。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Freaking product managers.
turns.zh: 该死的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: This is intuition. People just say, "Well, my [inaudible 01:00:30] was small, therefore I can still present the results." People want to see success. I mean, this is a natural bias, and then we have to be very conscientious and fight that bias and say when something looks too good to be true, investigate.
turns.zh: 这是直觉。人们就说“嗯，我的[听不清 01:00:30]很小，所以我仍然能展示结果。”人们想看到成功。我的意思是，这是个自然的偏见，然后我们得非常自觉地去对抗那个偏见，说当某物看起来好得不像真的，去调查。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which is a great segue to something you mentioned briefly, something called Twyman's law. Yeah. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 那是个很好的过渡，引向你简要提到过的、叫 Twyman 定律的东西。是的。你能聊聊那个吗？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah. So Twyman's law, the general statement is if any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong. It was first said by this person in the UK who worked in radio media, but I'm a big fan of it. And my main claim to people is if the result looks too good to be true, your normal movement of an experiment is under 1% and you suddenly have a 10% movement, hold the celebratory dinner. It was just your first reaction, right? Let's take everybody to a fancy dinner, because we just improved revenue by millions of dollars. Hold that dinner, investigate, see, because there's a large probability that something is wrong with the result. And I will say that nine out of 10, when we call it Twyman's law, it is the case that we find some flaw in the experiment.
turns.zh: 是的。所以 Twyman 定律，一般陈述是：任何看起来有趣或不同的数字通常都是错的。它最初由一个在英国做广播媒体的这人说的，而是它的忠实粉丝。而我对人们的主要主张是：如果结果好得不像真的，你实验的正常波动在 1% 以下、而你突然有了 10% 的波动，先别办那个庆祝晚宴。那只是你的第一反应，对吧？让我们带每个人去个高级餐厅，因为我们刚把收入改善了数百万美元。先别办那个晚宴，去调查、去看，因为结果有问题的概率很大。而我会说十次里有九次，当我们叫它 Twyman 定律时，确实是我们在实验里找到了某种缺陷。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Now there are obviously outliers. That first experiment that I shared where we promoted that made long titles, that was successful. But that was replicated multiple times, and double and triple checked, and everything was good about it. Many other results that were so big turn out to be false. So I'm a big fan of Twyman's law. There's a deck, I could also give this in the note, where I shared some real examples of Twyman's law.
turns.zh: 现在显然有异常值。我分享的第一个实验——我们提升让长标题——那是成功的。但那被重复了多次，并双重、三重检查了，而关于它一切都没问题。很多其他的、那么大的结果，结果证明是假的。所以我是 Twyman 定律的忠实粉丝。有个幻灯片，我也可以放在笔记里，我分享了一些 Twyman 定律的真实例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I want to talk about rolling this out of companies and things that you run into that fail. But before I get to that, I'd love for you to explain P value. I know that people kind of misunderstand it, and this might be a good time to just help people understand, what is it actually telling you, P value of say 0.05?
turns.zh: 惊人。我想聊聊把这个推到公司里、以及你遇到的失败的事。但在我到那之前，我很想让你解释 P 值。我知道人们有点误解它，而这可能正是个好时机帮人们理解，它实际在告诉你什么，比如 0.05 的 P 值？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I don't know if this is the right forum for explaining P values, because the definition of a P value is simple. What it hides is very complicated. So I'll say one thing, which is many people assign one minus P value as the probability that your treatment is better than control. So you ran an experiment, you got a P value of 0.02. They think there's a 98% probability that the treatment is better than the control. That is wrong. So rather than defining P values, I want to caution everybody that the most common interpretation is incorrect.
turns.zh: 我不知道这是不是解释 P 值的正确场合，因为 P 值的定义简单。它隐藏的非常复杂。所以我会说一件事，就是很多人把一减 P 值当成处理组优于对照组的概率。所以你跑了个实验，得到 0.02 的 P 值。他们认为有 98% 的概率处理组优于对照组。那是错的。所以与其定义 P 值，我想警告每个人：最普遍的解读是不正确的。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: P value assumes, it's a conditional probability or an assumed probability. It assumes that the null hypothesis is true. And we're computing the probability that the data we're seeing matches the hypothesis, this null hypothesis.
turns.zh: P 值假设——它是个条件概率或一个假定的概率。它假设零假设（null hypothesis）为真。而我们在计算我们看到的数据匹配那个假设、这个零假设的概率。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: In order to get the probability that most people want, we need to apply Bayes' rules and invert the probability from the probability of the data given the hypothesis, to the probability of the hypothesis given the data. For that, we need an additional number, which is the probability, the prior probability that the hypothesis that you're testing is successful or not.
turns.zh: 为了拿到大多数人想要的概率，我们需要应用贝叶斯法则，把概率从“给定假设的数据的概率”反转为“给定数据假设的概率”。为此，我们需要一个额外的数字，也就是那个先验概率——你正在测试的假设成功与否的概率。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: That's an unknown. What we do is we can take historical data and say, "Look, people fail two thirds of the time or 80% of the time." And we can apply that number and compute that. We've done that in a paper that I will give in the notes, so that you can assess the number that you really want, what's called a false positive risk.
turns.zh: 那是未知的。我们做的是我们可以拿历史数据说“看，人们三分之二的时候失败、或 80% 的时候失败。”而我们可以应用那个数字并计算。我们在一篇论文里做过那个，我会放在笔记里，这样你能评估你真正想要的数字——所谓的假阳性风险（false positive risk）。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So I think that's something for people to internalize, that what you really want to look at is this false positive risk, which tends to be much, much higher than the 5% that people think, right? So I think the classical example in the Airbnb where the failure rate was very, very high, is that when you get a statistically significant result, let me actually pull the note so that I know the actual number. If you're at Airbnb, or Airbnb search where the success rate is only 8%, if you get a statistically significant result with a P value less than 0.05, there is a 26% chance that this is a false positive result. It's not 5%, it's 26%.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得那是人们要内化的：你真正想看的是这个假阳性风险，它往往比人们以为的 5% 高得多，对吧？所以我觉得 Airbnb 那个经典例子——失败率非常高——是当你得到一个统计显著的结果，让我其实拉一下笔记好知道实际数字。如果你在 Airbnb，或 Airbnb 搜索——那里成功率只有 8%——如果你用小于 0.05 的 P 值得到一个统计显著的结果，有 26% 的概率是这是个假阳性结果。不是 5%，是 26%。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So that's the number that you should have in your mind. And that's why when I worked at Airbnb, one of the things we did is we said, "Okay, if you're less than 0.05, but above 0.01, rerun, replicate." When you replicate, you can combine the two experiments, and get a combined P value using something called Fisher's method or Stouffer's method, and that gives you the joint probability. And that's usually much, much lower. So if you get two 0.5's or something like that, then the probability that you've got them is much, much lower.
turns.zh: 所以那是你该记在脑子里的数字。而那也是为什么我在 Airbnb 时，我们做的一件事是我们说“好，如果你小于 0.05、但大于 0.01，重跑、复制。”当你复制时，你能结合两个实验，并用所谓的 Fisher 方法或 Stouffer 方法得到一个组合的 P 值，那给你联合概率。而那通常低得多。所以如果你得到两个 0.5 或类似，那么它们都出现的概率就低得多得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I've never heard it described that way. It makes me think about how even data scientists in our teams are always just like, "This isn't perfect. We're not 100% sure this experiment is positive." But on balance, if we're launching positive experiments, we're probably doing good things. It's okay if sometimes we're wrong.
turns.zh: 哇，我从没听过这样描述。它让我想到，即使我们团队里的数据科学家也总是像“这不完美。我们不 100% 确定这个实验是正向的。”但总的来说，如果我们发布正向的实验，我们大概在做好事。有时我们错也没关系。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: By the way, it's true. On balance, you're probably better than 50/50, but people don't appreciate how much that 26% that I mentioned is high. And the reason that I want to be sure is that I think it leads to this idea of the learning, the institutional knowledge. What you want to be able to say is share with the org's success. And so you want to be really sure that you're successful. So by lowering the P value, by forcing teams to work with the P value maybe below 0.01 and do replication on higher, then you can be much more successful, and the false positive rate will be much, much lower.
turns.zh: 顺便，那是真的。总的来说，你可能比 50/50 好，但人们不欣赏我提到的那个 26% 有多高。而我想确定的原因是，我觉得它引向这个学习和机构知识（institutional knowledge）的想法。你想要能说的是和组织的成功分享。所以你想真的确定你是成功的。所以通过降低 P 值、通过强迫团队用也许低于 0.01 的 P 值、并对更高的做复制，然后你能成功得多，而假阳性率会低得多得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fascinating. And also shows the value of keeping track of what percentage your experiments are failing historically at the company or within that specific product. Say someone listening wants to start running experiments, say they have tens of thousands of users at this point. What would be the first couple steps you'd recommend?
turns.zh: 迷人。而且也显示了跟踪“你们公司的实验历史上失败百分比是多少、或在那个特定产品里”的价值。假设有听众想开始跑实验，假设他们这会有数万用户了。你会推荐最先几步是什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Well, so if they have somebody in the org that has previously been involved with a experiment, that's a good way to consult internally. I think the key decision is whether you want to build or buy. There's a whole series of eight sessions that I posted on LinkedIn where I invited guest speakers to talk about this problem. So if people are interested, they can look at what the vendors say and what agency said about build versus buy question. And it's usually not a zero one, it's usually both. You build some and you buy some, and it's a question of do you build 10% or do you build in 90%?
turns.zh: 嗯，所以如果他们组织里有人之前参与过实验，那是个很好的内部咨询方式。我觉得关键决定是你想自建还是买。我发在 LinkedIn 上有一整套八个 session，我邀请了客座讲者聊这个问题。所以如果人们感兴趣，他们能看供应商和在 build vs buy 问题上机构说了什么。而它通常不是非黑即白，通常两者都有。你建一些、买一些，而问题是你建 10% 还是建 90%？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I think for people starting, the third party products that are available today are pretty good. This wasn't the case when I started working. So when I started running experiments at Amazon, we were building the platform because nothing existed. Same at Microsoft. I think today, there's enough vendors that provide good experimentation platforms that are trustworthy, that I would say not a good way to consider using one of those.
turns.zh: 我觉得对起步的人，今天可用的第三方产品相当好。在我开始工作那会不是这样。所以当我开始在 Amazon 跑实验时，我们在建平台因为什么都不存在。微软也一样。我觉得今天，有足够多的供应商提供可信赖的好实验平台，而我会说不考虑用其中一个不是个好方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say you're at a company where there's resistance to experimentation and A/B testing, whether it's a startup or a bigger company. What have you found works in helping shift that culture, and how long does that usually take, especially at a larger company?
turns.zh: 假设你在一家对实验和 A/B 测试有阻力的公司，无论它是创业公司还是更大的公司。你发现什么在帮助转变那种文化上有效，而那通常要多久，尤其在大公司？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: My general experience is with Microsoft, where we went with this beach head of Bing. We were running a few experiments and then we were asked to focus on Bing, and we scaled experimentation and built a platform at scale at Bing.
turns.zh: 我的总体经验是在微软，我们走的是 Bing 这个滩头堡（beach head）。我们跑了一些实验，然后被要求聚焦在 Bing，而我们在 Bing 规模化了实验、并建了一个规模化的平台。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Once Bing was successful and we were able to share all these surprising results, I think that many, many more people in the company were amenable. It was also the case that helped a lot that, there's a usual cross pollination. People from Bing move out to other groups, and that helped these other groups say, "Hey, there's a better way to build software."
turns.zh: 一旦 Bing 成功了、而我们能分享所有这些令人惊讶的结果，我觉得公司里很多、很多人变得能接受了。还有个情况也帮了大忙，就是通常的cross pollination（交叉传播）。Bing 的人挪到其他组，那帮了那些别的组说“嘿，有种更好的方式建软件。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So I think if you're starting out, find a place, find a team where experimentation is easy to run. And by that, I mean they're launching often, right? Don't go with the team that launches every six months, or Office used to launch every three years. Go with the team that launches frequently. They're running on sprints, they launch every week or two. Sometimes they launch daily. I mean, Bing used to launch multiple times a day.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得如果你在起步，找到一个地方、找到一个容易跑实验的团队。而我意思是他们经常发布，对吧？别去那个每六个月才发布的团队，或 Office 以前每三年发布。去那个频繁发布的团队。他们在 sprint 上跑，每一两周发布。有时他们每天发布。我的意思是，Bing 以前一天发布好几次。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And then make sure that you understand the question of the OEC. Is it clear what they're optimizing for? There are some groups where you can come up with a good OEC. Some groups are harder.
turns.zh: 然后确保你理解 OEC 的问题。他们在优化什么清楚吗？有些组你能想出一个好的 OEC。有些组更难。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I remember one funny example was the microsoft.com website, which this is not MSN, this is microsoft.com, has multiple different constituencies that are trying to determine this is a support site, and this is the ability to sell software through this site, and warn you about safety and updates. It has so many goals. I remember when the team said, "We want to run experiments," and I brought the group in and some of the managers and I said, "Do you know what you're optimizing for?"
turns.zh: 我记得一个好笑的例子是 microsoft.com 网站——这不是 MSN，这是 microsoft.com——有多个不同的受众在试图决定这是个支持站点、以及这是个通过这个站点卖软件的能力、并警告你安全和更新。它有太多目标。我记得当团队说“我们想跑实验”，而我带了组里一些人、一些经理进来，我说“你们知道你们在优化什么吗？”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: It was very funny because they surprised me. They said, "Hey Ronny, we read some of your papers. We know there's this term called OEC. We decided the time on site is our OEC." And I said, "Wait a minute. Some of your main goals is support site. Is people spending more time on the support site a good thing or a bad thing?" And then half the room thought that more time is better, and half the room thought that more time is worse. So an OEC is bad if directionally, you can't agree on it.
turns.zh: 很好笑因为他们让我惊讶。他们说“嘿 Ronny，我们读了你的一些论文。我们知道有个词叫 OEC。我们决定了停留时间（time on site）是我们的 OEC。”而我说“等一下。你们主要目标之一是支持站点。人们在支持站点上花更多时间是好事还是坏事？”然后半个房间觉得更多时间更好、半个房间觉得更多时间更糟。所以一个 OEC 如果在方向上你不能达成一致，就是个坏的 OEC。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great tip. Along these same lines, I know you're a big fan of platforms and building a platform to run experiments, versus just one-off experiments. Can you just talk briefly about that to give people a sense of where they probably should be going with their experimentation approach?
turns.zh: 那是个很棒的建议。沿着这些线，我知道你是平台的大粉丝、以及建一个平台来跑实验，而不是只跑一次性实验。你能简短聊聊那个，给人们一种他们大概该把实验方式带向哪里的感觉吗？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah, so I think the motivation is to bring the marginal cost of experiments down to zero. So the more you self-service, go to a website, set up your experiment, define your targets, define the metrics that you want, right? People don't appreciate that the number of metrics starts to grow really fast if you're doing things right. At Bing, you could define 10,000 metrics that you wanted to be in your scorecard. Big numbers.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我觉得动机是把实验的边际成本降到零。所以你自助服务越多——去个网站、设好你的实验、定义你的目标、定义你想要的指标，对吧？人们不欣赏的是，如果你做得对，指标的数量开始增长得非常快。在 Bing，你能定义 1 万个你想放进你记分卡的指标。大数字。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So it was so big, and people said it's computationally inefficient. We broke them into templates so that if you were launching a UI experiment, you would get this set of 2,000. If you were doing a revenue experiment, you would get this set of 2,000.
turns.zh: 所以它那么大，而人们说它计算上低效。我们把它们拆成模板，这样如果你在发布一个 UI 实验，你会得到这套 2000 个。如果你在做收入实验，你会得到这套 2000 个。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So the point was build a platform that can quickly allow you to set up and run an experiment, and then analyze it. I think one of the things that I will say at Airbnb is the analysis was relatively weak, and so lots of data scientists were hired to be able to compensate for the fact that the platform didn't do enough.
turns.zh: 所以重点是建一个平台，能让你快速设立并跑一个实验，然后分析它。我觉得在 Airbnb 我会说的一件事是分析相对弱，所以雇了很多数据科学家来补偿平台做得不够的事实。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And this happens in other organizations too, where there's this trade-off. If you're building a good platform, invest in it so that more and more automation will allow people to look at the analysis, without the need to involve a data scientist.
turns.zh: 而这也在其他组织发生，那里有这个权衡。如果你在建一个好的平台，投资在它上面，这样越来越多的自动化能让人们看分析、而不需要涉及数据科学家。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: We published a paper. Again, I'll give it in the notes with this nice matrix of six axes, and how you move from crawl, to walk, to run, to fly, and what you need to build on those six axes. So one of the things that I do sometimes when I consult is I go into the org and say, "Where do you think you are on these six axes?" And that should be the guidance for what are the things you need to do next.
turns.zh: 我们发表了篇论文。再次，我会在笔记里给它——有个漂亮的六轴矩阵，以及你怎么从爬、走到跑、到飞，以及你在那些六轴上需要建什么。所以我咨询时有时做的一件事是，我进到组织说“你觉得你们在这六轴上在哪？”而那应该是你下一步需要做什么的指导。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is going to be the most epic show notes episode we've had yet. Maybe a last question. We talked about how important trust is to running experiments, and how even though people talk about speed, trust ends up being most important. Still, I want to ask you about speed. Is there anything you recommend for helping people run experiments faster and get results more quickly that they can implement?
turns.zh: 这会是我们有过最史诗的节目笔记一期。可能是最后一个问题。我们聊了信任对跑实验多重要、以及即使人们聊速度、信任最终最重要。尽管如此，我想问你关于速度。有没有你推荐的、帮助人们更快跑实验、更快拿到结果、而且他们能实现的东西？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yeah, so I'll say a couple of things. One is if your platform is good, then when the experiment finishes, you should have a scorecard soon after. Maybe takes a day, but it shouldn't be that you have to wait a week for the data scientist. To me, this is the number one way to speed up things.
turns.zh: 是的，所以我会说几件事。一个是如果你的平台好，那么当实验结束时，你应该不久后就有个记分卡。也许花一天，但不该是你得等数据科学家一周。对我来说，这是加速的头号方式。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Now, in terms of using the data efficiently, there are mechanisms out there under the title of variance reduction that help you reduce the variance of metrics so that you need less users, so that you can get results faster. Some examples that you might think about are capping metrics. So if your revenue metric is very skewed, maybe you say, "Well, if somebody purchased over $1,000, let's make that $1,000." At Airbnb, one of the key metrics for example, is nights booked.
turns.zh: 现在，在高效使用数据方面，有些叫方差缩减（variance reduction）的机制，帮你减少指标的方差，这样你需要更少的用户，这样你能更快拿到结果。你可能会想的一些例子是给指标封顶（capping）。所以如果你的收入指标非常偏斜，也许你说“嗯，如果有人买了超过 1000 美元，我们就让那是 1000 美元。”在 Airbnb，一个关键指标比如是预订夜数（nights booked）。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Well, it turns out that some people book tens of nights. They're like an agency or something, hundreds of nights. You may say, "Okay, let's just cap this. It's unlikely that people book more than 30 days in a given month." So that various reduction technique will allow you to get statistically significant results faster.
turns.zh: 嗯，结果有些人订几十晚。他们像个机构或什么，几百晚。你可能会说“好，我们就封顶这个。人们在一个给定月份订超过 30 天不太可能。”所以那个各种缩减技术会让你更快得到统计显著的结果。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And a third technique is called cupid, which is an article that we published. Again, I can give it in the notes, which uses the pre-experiment data to adjust the result. And we can show that you get the result as unbiased, but with lower variance, and hence, it requires fewer users.
turns.zh: 而第三个技术叫 cupid，是我们发表的一篇文章。再次，我能在笔记里给它，它用实验前的数据来调整结果。而我们能展示你得到的结果是无偏的，但方差更低，因此，它需要更少的用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ronny, is there anything else you want to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: Ronny，在我们进入非常令人兴奋的闪电轮之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: No, I think we've asked a lot of good questions. Hope people enjoy this.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得我们已经问了很多好问题。希望人们喜欢这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know they will.
turns.zh: 我知道他们会。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Lightning round.
turns.zh: 闪电轮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Lightning round. Here we go. I'm just going to roll right into it. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 闪电轮。我们开始。我直接进去。你最常推荐给其他人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: There's a fun book called Calling Bullshit, which despite the name, which is a little extreme, I think, for a title, it actually has a lot of amazing insights that I love. And it sort of embodies, in my opinion, a lot of the Twyman's law showing that things that are too extreme, your bullshit meter should go up and say, "Hey, I don't believe that." So that's my number one recommendation.
turns.zh: 有本有趣的书叫《Calling Bullshit（胡说八道）》（尽管这名字，对我来说作为标题有点极端），它其实有很多我爱的惊人洞见。而在我看来，它某种程度上体现了很多 Twyman 定律——那些太极端的东西，你的胡说八道探测器该升起来说“嘿，我不信那个。”所以那是我的头号推荐。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: There's a slightly older book that I love called Hard Facts, Dangerous Half-Truths And Total Nonsense by the Stanford professors from the Graduate School of Business. Very interesting to see many of the things that we grew up with as well understood turn out to have no justification.
turns.zh: 有本稍老点的书我很爱，叫《Hard Facts, Dangerous Half-Truths And Total Nonsense（硬事实、危险的一半真相和彻头彻尾的胡说）》，作者是斯坦福商学院的教授。看到很多我们从小以为是well understood的东西、结果毫无依据，很有趣。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So a stranger book, which I love, sort of on the verge of psychology, it's called Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me), about all the fallacies that we fall into, and the humbling results from that.
turns.zh: 所以一本更陌生的书，我很爱，有点在心理学边缘，叫《Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)（错误被犯下了（但不是我犯的））》，关于我们掉进去的所有谬误，以及从中得出的让人谦卑的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The titles of these are hilarious, and there's a common theme across all these books. Next question, what is a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 这些书的标题都好笑，而这些书之间有个共同的主题。下一个问题，最近喜欢的电影或剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So I recently saw a short series called Chernobyl, the disaster. I thought it was amazingly well done. Highly recommended it, based on true events. As usual, there's some freedom for the artistic movie. It was kind of interesting at the end, they say, "This woman in the movie wasn't really a woman. It was a bunch of 30 data scientists." Not data scientists, 30 scientists that in real life, presented all the data to the leadership of what to do.
turns.zh: 所以我最近看了一个短剧叫《Chernobyl（切尔诺贝利）》，那场灾难。我觉得它做得惊人地好。强烈推荐，基于真实事件。像通常那样，电影在艺术上有一些自由发挥。有趣的是最后他们说“电影里那个女人其实不是个女人。那是一群 30 个数据科学家。”不是数据科学家，是 30 个科学家，现实中，向领导层展示了所有该做什么的数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember that. Fun fact, I was born in Odessa, Ukraine, which was not so far from Chernobyl. And I remember my dad told me he had to go to work. They called him into work that day to clean some stuff off the trees. I think ash from the explosion or something. It was far away where I don't think we were exposed, but we were in the vicinity. That's pretty scary. My wife, every time something's wrong with me, she's like, "That must be a Chernobyl thing." Okay, next question. Favorite interview question you like to ask people when you're interviewing them?
turns.zh: 我记得那个。趣闻，我出生在乌克兰的敖德萨（Odessa），离切尔诺贝利不算远。而我记得我爸告诉我他那天得去上班。他们那天把他叫去上班，去清理树上的一些东西。我想是爆炸的灰或什么。它离得远，我觉得我们没暴露，但我们在附近。那挺吓人。我妻子，每次我有点不对劲，她就“那肯定是切尔诺贝利的事。”好的，下一个问题。面试别人时你喜欢问的、最喜欢的一个面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So it depends on the interview, but when I do a technical interview, which I do less of, but one question that I love that it's amazing how many people it throws away for languages like C++, is tell me what the static qualifier does. And for multiple, you can do it for a variable, you can do it for function. And it is just amazing that I would say more than 50% of people that interview for engineering job cannot get this, and get it awfully wrong.
turns.zh: 所以看面试，但当我做技术面试——我做这比较少——但我爱的一个问题，惊人的是它难倒了多少人，尤其是对 C++ 这样的语言——告诉我 static 限定符（qualifier）做什么。而对多个，你可以对一个变量做、你可以对一个函数做。而就是惊人的是，我会说面试工程岗的人里超过 50% 答不上来这个，而且答得离谱地错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Definitely the most technical answer to this question yet.
turns.zh: 绝对是到目前为止对这个问题最技术性的回答。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Very technical, yeah.
turns.zh: 非常技术，是的。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I love it.
turns.zh: 我爱这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. What's a favorite recent product you've discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 好的。最近发现、并喜欢的一个最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Blink cameras. So a Blink camera is this small camera. You stick in two AA batteries, and it lasts for about six months. They claim up to two years. My experience is usually about six months. But it was just amazing to me how you can throw these things around in the yard and see things that you would never know otherwise. Some animals that go by. We had a skunk that we couldn't figure out how he was entering, so I threw five cameras out and I saw where he came in.
turns.zh: Blink 摄像头。所以一个 Blink 摄像头就是这种小摄像头。你塞两节 AA 电池进去，它能撑大约六个月。他们声称长达两年。我的经验通常大约六个月。但它让我惊讶的是，你能把这些东西随便扔在院子里、看到你否则永远不会知道的东西。一些经过的动物。我们有只臭鼬，我们搞不清它是怎么进来的，所以我扔了五个摄像头出去，然后我看到了它从哪进来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where'd he come in?
turns.zh: 它从哪进来？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: He came in under a hole on the fence that was about this high. I have a video of this thing just squishing underneath. We never would've assumed that it came from there, from the neighbor. But yeah, these things have just changed. And when you're away on a trip, it's always nice to be able to say, "I can see my house. Everything's okay." At one point, we had a false alarm, and the cops came in and had this amazing video of how they're entering the house and pulling the guns out.
turns.zh: 它从围栏上一个大约这么高的洞钻进来。我有段视频，这家伙就那样挤在下面。我们绝不会假设它是从那、从邻居那来的。但是的，这些东西就是改变了。而当你外出旅行时，能说“我能看到我家。一切都好”总是很好。有一回，我们误报了，警察来了，还有段惊人的视频，关于他们怎么进屋、把枪掏出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You got to share that on TikTok. That's good content. Wow. Okay. Blink cameras. We'll set those up in my house asap.
turns.zh: 你得在 TikTok 上分享那个。那是好内容。哇。好的。Blink 摄像头。我们会尽快在我家装上。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is something relatively minor you've changed in the way your teams develop product, that has had a big impact on their ability to execute?
turns.zh: 有什么相对小的、你改变团队开发产品方式的做法，却对他们执行能力有重大影响？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I think this is something that I learned at Amazon, which is a structured narrative. So Amazon has some variance of this, which sometimes go by the name of a six pager or something. But when I was at Amazon, I still remember that email from Jeff, which is, "No more PowerPoint. I'm going to force you to write a narrative."
turns.zh: 我觉得这是我在 Amazon 学到的，叫结构化叙述（structured narrative）。所以 Amazon 有这个的一些变体，有时叫六页纸（six pager）或类似。但我在 Amazon 时，我还记得 Jeff 的那封邮件，就是“不要 PowerPoint 了。我要逼你们写个叙述。”

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I took that to heart. And many of the features that the team presented instead of a PowerPoint, you start off with a structured document that tells you what you need, the questions you need to answer for your idea. And then we review them as a team.
turns.zh: 我把那个记在心里。而团队展示的很多功能，不靠 PowerPoint，而是从一个结构化文档开始，告诉你你需要什么、你的想法需要回答的问题。然后我们作为一个团队评审它们。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: And Amazon, these were paper-based. Now it's all based on Word or Google Docs where people comment, and I think the impact of that was amazing. I think the ability to give people honest feedback and have them appreciate, and have it stay after the meeting in these notes on the document, just amazing.
turns.zh: 而在 Amazon，这些是基于纸的。现在都基于 Word 或 Google Docs，人们在上面评论，而我觉得那的影响惊人。我觉得给人们诚实反馈的能力、并让他们欣赏、并且让它在会议后留在文档的这些笔记里，就惊人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, have you ever run an A/B test on your life, either your dating life, your family, your kids? And if so, what did you try?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，你有没有在你的人生上跑过 A/B 测试——无论是你的约会生活、你的家庭、你的孩子？如果有，你试了什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: So there aren't enough units. Remember I said you need 10,000 of something to run true A/B tests? I will say a couple of things. One is I try to emphasize to my family, and friends, and everybody, this idea called the hierarchy of evidence. When you read something, there's a hierarchy of trust levels. If something is anecdotal, don't trust it. If there was an experiment, it was observational. Give it some bit of trust. As you get more up and up to a natural experiment, and controlled experiments, and multiple controlled experiments, your trust levels should go up. So I think that that's a very important thing that a lot of people miss when they see something in the news is, where does it come from?
turns.zh: 所以没有足够的单元。记得我说你需要 1 万个单位才能跑真正的 A/B 测试？我会说几件事。一个是我想对我的家人、朋友、和每个人强调，这个叫证据层级（hierarchy of evidence）的想法。当你读到某物，有个信任级别的层级。如果某物是轶事的，别信它。如果有实验，它是观察性的。给它一点信任。当你越往上到自然实验、受控实验、多个受控实验，你的信任级别该上去。所以我觉得那是很多人看到新闻里某物时漏掉的、非常重要的事——它从哪来？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: I have a talk that I've shared of all these observational studies that people made that were published. And then somehow, a control experiment was run later on and proved that it was directionally incorrect. So I think there's a lot to learn about this idea of the hierarchy of evidence, and share it with our family, and kids, and friends. I think there's a book that's based on this. It's like How to Read a Book.
turns.zh: 我有个分享过的演讲，关于所有这些人们做并发表了的观察性研究。然后不知怎的，后来跑了个受控实验，证明它在方向上是错的。所以我觉得关于这个证据层级的想法有很多可学，并与我们的家人、孩子、朋友分享。我觉得有本基于这个的书。它像《How to Read a Book（如何读一本书）》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, Ronny, the experiment of us recording a podcast I think is 100% positive P value 0.0. Thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 好，Ronny，我们录这期播客的实验我觉得是 100% 正向、P 值 0.0。非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Thank you so much for inviting me and for great questions.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你邀请我、以及这些好问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I appreciate that. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, and is there anything that listeners can do for you?
turns.zh: 惊人。我感激那个。两个最后的问题。如果人们想联系，能在哪找到你，以及听众能为你做什么？

turns.speaker: Ronny Kohavi
turns.en: Finding me online is easy. It's LinkedIn. And what can people do for me? Understand the idea of control experiments as a mechanism to make the right data-driven decisions. Use science. Learn more by reading my book if you want. Again, all proceeds go to charity. And if you want to learn more, there's a class that I teach every quarter on Maven. We'll put in the notes how to find it, and some discount for people who managed to stay all the way to the end of this podcast.
turns.zh: 在网上找到我很容易。是 LinkedIn。而人们能为我做什么？理解受控实验这个想法，作为一种做正确数据驱动决策的机制。用科学。想的话通过读我的书学更多。再次，所有收益都归慈善。而如果你想学更多，我每个季度在 Maven 上教一门课。我们会把怎么找到它放进笔记，以及一些给那些设法坚持到这期播客结尾的人的折扣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's awesome. We'll include that at the top so people don't miss it, so there's going to be a code to get a discount on your course. Ronny, thank you again so much for being here. This was amazing.
turns.zh: 是的，那超棒。我们会把它放在最上面，这样人们不会错过，所以会有一个代码来给你的课程打折。Ronny，再次非常感谢你来到这里。这太棒了。
